Your Muscles Shrink After 60! 💪 Add This To Coffee OR Keep Losing Muscle Mass ☕ | Dr. Jason Fung


Have you noticed that climbing stairs feels harder, your grip is weaker, or everyday activities require more effort than they once did? After age 60, maintaining muscle mass becomes increasingly important for independence, balance, mobility, and healthy aging. Age-related muscle loss, known as **sarcopenia**, can gradually affect strength and quality of life—but the right combination of nutrition, physical activity, and healthy habits may help you protect your muscles and stay active for years to come.

In this educational video, we explore how your morning coffee could become an opportunity to support a muscle-friendly nutrition routine. ☕💪 Discover the science behind protein intake, essential nutrients, muscle protein synthesis, and resistance exercise. We will also examine whether adding a protein-rich ingredient to coffee makes sense for older adults, why coffee alone cannot prevent muscle loss, and how to make smarter dietary choices after 60.

01:20 – 🧬 Understanding Age-Related Muscle Loss

17:00 – 🌟 Your Healthy Aging Action Plan  
17:40 – ❤️ Final Thoughts: Strength for Life

subtitles.plaintext:
Quit stirring sugar and creamer into
your morning coffee and calling it
breakfast. If you are over 60, that cup
in your hand is either the most wasted
opportunity of your day or the easiest
muscle building habit you will ever
adopt. And the difference comes down to
what you put in it. Nobody in the
supplement aisle will explain this to
you. And most of your doctors simply
have not had time to. Today I'm going to
show you six simple additions to your
coffee that support the muscles that
keep you standing, walking, and living
on your own terms. Before we dive in,
take a moment to subscribe to my channel
and tell me in the comments where you
are watching from today.
Let me start with a number that should
get your attention. Research on aging
shows that after about age 30, adults
lose roughly 3 to 8% of their muscle
mass every decade. And that loss speeds
up after 60. A large meta-analysis
published in the British Journal of
Sports Medicine, which pulled 49 studies
and more than 1,800 participants, found
that adequate protein combined with
resistance exercise measurably increased
muscle strength and size even in older
adults. The problem is that most seniors
are not getting enough of the right
nutrients at the right time. Your
muscles are not gone, my friend. They
are waiting for the right signal. And
your morning coffee is the perfect
delivery vehicle for that signal because
you are already doing it every single
day. Think of your muscles like a house
that is constantly being repaired by a
small crew of workers. When you are
young, that crew shows up early, works
fast, and brings all the materials they
need. After 60, the crew still shows up,
but they are slower. They need more
materials, and they need a louder
wake-up call. Doctors call this anabolic
resistance, which simply means your
aging muscles respond less strongly to
the protein you eat than they did when
you were 30. The good news is that you
can overcome it. And these six coffee
additions are how.
Now, I promised you six, and I am going
to count them down from the least
powerful to the most powerful. But, I
want you to stay until the very end
because number one is something almost
everyone adds to coffee the wrong way.
Do it right and you get a real
advantage. Do it wrong and you throw
most of the benefit away. I will show
you exactly how at the end. Before we
start, I would love to know two things.
Tell me your age in the comments, and
tell me what is in your coffee right
now. Is it sugar, creamer, nothing at
all? I read every single comment, and
your answers help me decide which videos
to make next. Let us begin with number
six. Cinnamon. Cinnamon may seem like a
humble kitchen spice, but it plays a
surprisingly interesting role for aging
muscles. As we get older, many of us
become less sensitive to insulin, the
hormone that moves sugar out of the
blood and into our cells, including our
muscle cells. When that process slows
down, your muscles get less fuel, and
over time, blood sugar climbs. Several
clinical trials and reviews have found
that cinnamon can modestly improve
fasting blood sugar and insulin
sensitivity in some adults, particularly
those with elevated blood sugar. The
effect is not dramatic, and I want about
that, but it is real enough to be worth
a pinch of spice.
Think of insulin like a key, and your
muscle cell like a locked door. With
age, the lock gets a little rusty.
Cinnamon does not replace the key, but
it may help oil the lock so that fuel
and nutrients enter more easily. I think
of a retired school teacher named
Margaret, 73, from Asheville, North
Carolina. She told me her afternoons
were a fog of fatigue and she was always
reaching for something sweet around
3:00. Her morning coffee was loaded with
two spoonfuls of sugar. She swapped the
sugar for half a teaspoon of cinnamon
and began a short walk after breakfast.
Within 2 months she told me her
afternoon crashes had faded and she was
finally able to carry her own groceries
up the porch steps again. Her muscles
did not magically return overnight, but
steady energy meant she moved more and
moving more is what protects muscle.
Here is how to use it. Stir half a
teaspoon of Ceylon cinnamon into your
coffee or sprinkle it on top of the
grounds before brewing. I recommend
Ceylon, sometimes called true cinnamon,
over the common cassia variety because
cassia contains a compound called
coumarin that can stress the liver in
large amounts. For your best timing,
have it with your morning cup alongside
some protein. And for the synergy tip,
pair cinnamon with a little fat such as
a splash of whole milk which helps carry
its aromatic compounds and makes the cup
far more satisfying. On to number five,
unsweetened cocoa powder.
Chocolate lovers, this one is for you.
But I am not talking about candy or
sweetened hot chocolate. I mean plain
unsweetened cocoa powder which is rich
in natural plant compounds called
flavanols. Flavanols are antioxidants
that help your blood vessels relax and
widen. And that matters for muscles in a
way most people never consider. Your
muscles are fed by blood. Every
nutrient, every amino acid, every bit of
oxygen travels through your bloodstream
to reach them. Studies on cocoa
flavanols have shown improvements in
blood vessel function and blood flow in
older adults and better circulation
means more delivery to the tissues that
need repair. Picture your blood vessels
as a delivery road. With age, that road
narrows and gets bumpy, so the trucks
carrying protein and oxygen move slowly.
Cocoa flavanols may help widen the road
and smooth it out so the trucks arrive
on time. Let me tell you about Walter,
78, from Tulsa, Oklahoma.
Walter was a retired machinist who told
me his legs felt heavy and tired
whenever he climbed stairs. His doctor
had told him to be more active, but he
had no energy. He started adding a
heaping teaspoon of unsweetened cocoa
powder to his morning coffee along with
a daily walk around the block. After
about 6 weeks, he told me the walks went
from one block to four. I cannot promise
that cocoa did all of that, and Walter
would be the first to credit the
walking, but he believed the combination
changed how his legs felt, and I believe
him. For preparation, whisk one heaping
teaspoon of unsweetened cocoa powder
into a little hot water first to make a
smooth paste, then pour in your coffee.
This stops it from clumping at the top.
Take it in the morning because cocoa
does contain a small amount of caffeine,
and you do not want it to disturb your
sleep. For your synergy tip, combine it
with cinnamon because the two flavors
work beautifully together and with a
source of protein because better blood
flow is only useful if there is
something worth delivering. Now, let us
move to number four, collagen peptides.
You have probably heard of collagen for
skin and joints, but here is something
that surprises most people. Collagen is
also a major structural protein in the
connective tissue that surrounds and
holds your muscle fibers together. A
well-known German study from the
University of Freiburg looked at older
men with sarcopenia, which is the
medical word for age-related muscle
loss. For 12 weeks, the men did
resistance training, and half of them
took 15 g of collagen peptides daily
while while the other half took a
placebo. The collagen group gained more
muscle mass and lost more fat than the
placebo group. It was a small study and
it needs more research, but it was a
striking result. Here is the catch I
want you to hear clearly. Collagen alone
is not a complete protein. It is low in
an amino acid called leucine, which is
the key that switches on muscle
building. So, think of collagen as the
scaffolding, not the whole construction
crew. It supports the structure around
your muscle, but does not replace the
full protein you need from food. I want
to introduce you to Dolores, 71, from
Albuquerque, New Mexico. She struggled
with stiff knees and told me she felt
wobbly on stairs. She began mixing one
scoop of collagen peptides into her
coffee every morning and she added two
simple strength exercises, standing up
from a chair and wall push-ups. After 3
months, she told me her knees felt
steadier and she was no longer gripping
the railing like a lifeline. To prepare
it, choose unflavored collagen peptides,
which dissolve easily in hot coffee
without clumping. Use 10 to 15 g, which
is about one to two scoops, depending on
the brand. Take it in the morning,
ideally within an hour of exercise if
you exercise. For your synergy tip, pair
collagen with vitamin C, which your body
needs to build collagen properly. A
glass of orange juice or a few
strawberries alongside your coffee does
the job nicely.
Now, before we move on to the top three,
let me ask you a quick favor. If this
video is already teaching you something
new, please tap the like button, please
subscribe, and hit the bell. It is free.
It takes 2 seconds and it helps this
channel reach more seniors who deserve
to hear this information. Every week, I
bring you practical science-based ways
to protect your muscles, your heart, and
your independence. Thank you for being
here. Now, let us get to the best of the
best. Number three is creatine. Yes,
creatine. Most people hear that word and
picture young bodybuilders in a gym, but
creatine is one of the most studied
supplements in the world, and some of
its most interesting research is in
older adults. Creatine is a natural
compound stored in your muscles that
helps produce quick bursts
As we age, our muscle creatine stores
decline. Multiple meta-analyses of
clinical trials have found that older
adults who took creatine while doing
resistance training gained more lean
mass and strength than those who trained
without it. Researchers have also been
studying its potential benefits for bone
health and even brain function, though
that research is still developing. Think
of creatine like a small rechargeable
battery inside each muscle cell. When
the battery is full, your muscles can
push harder and recover faster. After
60, those batteries drain faster and
recharge more slowly. Creatine helps
refill them. I think of Harold 76 from
Duluth, Minnesota. He was a retired
postal carrier who told me he had gotten
so weak that he struggled to get out of
his favorite armchair. His doctor
cleared him to try 3 g of creatine daily
along with a simple resistance band
routine. After 4 months, Harold told me
he could stand up from the chair without
using his hands, and he told me that
felt like winning the lottery. For
preparation, the typical amount studied
is 3 to 5 g, roughly 1 tsp of creatine
monohydrate. It dissolves easily in
coffee, and the old worry that caffeine
cancels creatine has not held up well in
more recent research. Take it every day
because the benefit comes from keeping
your stores topped up, not from one big
dose. For your synergy tip, take it
alongside a source of carbohydrate or
protein, such as the milk or protein we
will talk about shortly, which may help
muscles absorb it. One important caution
though, if you have kidney disease or
any kidney concerns, speak with your
doctor before taking creatine. Please do
not skip that step. Now, number two,
milk, specifically whole or fortified
milk. I know it sounds simple, but stay
with me. Cow's milk is one of the most
underrated muscle foods in the world. It
contains high-quality protein rich in
that muscle switch amino acid I
mentioned, leucine. It also contains
calcium and in most countries it is
fortified with vitamin D. Two nutrients
your bones and muscles are both
desperate for after 60. Vitamin D
deficiency is very common among older
adults and low levels have been linked
in observational research with weaker
muscles and a higher risk of falls. A
glass of milk delivers roughly 8 g of
protein. So, a generous splashing
coffee, or better yet, making a latte
style cup with a full cup of milk adds a
meaningful amount. Here's the analogy.
If your muscle is a house being
repaired, then protein is the lumber and
leucine is the foreman who shouts,
"Start building." Now, milk delivers
both plus the calcium and vitamin D that
hold the foundation up. Let me tell you
about Evelyn, 82, from Burlington,
Vermont. She was a retired nurse who
lost nearly all her appetite after her
husband passed and she was living on tea
and toast. Her daughter noticed she was
getting frail. Evelyn began making her
morning coffee as a latte with a full
cup of warm milk. It was easy,
comforting, and she could manage it.
Within a few months, she was stronger.
Her doctor was pleased with her weight,
and she told me she was finally back in
her garden. Sometimes the simplest
changes are the ones people actually
stick with. For preparation, use whole
or 2% milk if your doctor approves, or
an unsweetened fortified soy milk if you
prefer a plant option, since soy is the
plant milk closest to cow's milk in
protein. If dairy gives you trouble,
lactose-free milk has the same protein.
Warm it gently and pour it into your
coffee, aiming for about 1 cup. Take it
in the morning and consider a second
glass later in the day. For your synergy
tip, pair milk with a short walk after
your coffee, because gentle movement
helps your muscles use the amino acids
you have just supplied. And now, number
one, the most powerful addition you can
make to your coffee protein powder,
specifically whey protein. Here is why
it takes the top spot. Of everything on
this list, nothing speaks directly to
anabolic resistance the way a high dose
of leucine-rich protein does.
Researchers have found that older adults
need a larger dose of protein per minute
yield than younger adults to switch on
muscle building, often at least 25 to 30
g, which includes roughly 2 and 1/2 to 3
g of leucine. Whey protein is one of the
richest and fastest digesting sources of
leucine available. Studies in older
adults have shown that supplementing
with whey protein, especially alongside
resistance exercise, can improve muscle
mass and strength. And here is a problem
that almost no one talks about. Most
seniors eat a tiny amount of protein at
breakfast, perhaps toast and coffee,
which is maybe 5 to 10 g. That is far
below the amount your aging muscles need
to respond. A scoop of whey in your
coffee fixes that gap in about 30
seconds. Think of it like this. Your
muscles after 60 are like a car that
needs a stronger push to start. A small
amount of protein is a gentle nudge and
the car does not move. A full dose of 25
to 30 g is a strong push that finally
gets the engine running. I want to share
the story of George, 79, from Savannah,
Georgia. He was a retired electrician
who told me his legs had weakened so
much that he was afraid to walk his dog.
He had been eating toast and black
coffee for breakfast every morning for
40 years. George began blending one
scoop of unflavored whey protein into a
cooled cup of coffee each morning and
began walking a little farther each day.
After 5 months, he told me he was
walking his dog twice a day and had
started carrying his own groceries
again. He said he He said to me,
"Doctor, I didn't know my body still had
that in it."
It always did, my friend. It just needed
the right signal.
Now, here is the part I promised. The
mistake almost everyone makes is pouring
protein powder straight into piping hot
coffee. Whey protein can clump and
curdle in very hot liquid, which makes
it gritty and unpleasant, and many
people give up after one bad cup.
Instead, let your coffee cool for a few
minutes until it is warm rather than
scalding. Add your scoop of powder to a
shaker or blender, pour in a little
cooled coffee, mix it into a smooth
paste, then add the rest or blend it
with iced protein coffee. Aim for 25 to
30 g of protein, which is usually one
scoop. Take it at breakfast cuz that is
the meal where most seniors are shortest
on protein. For your synergy tip,
combine it with the milk from number two
and a sprinkle of the cinnamon from
number six, and you have a drink that
works on several fronts at once. If you
have kidney disease, please check with
your doctor about your protein intake
before making changes. So, that is the
list. In reverse order, whey protein,
milk, creatine, collagen peptides,
cocoa, and cinnamon. Six simple
additions to the cup you already drink
every morning. And remember, the
research behind these claims is linked
in the description below. So, please
take a look and share it with your
doctor. I want to leave you with
something I feel deeply. Your muscles
are not just about strength. They are
about independence. They are the
difference between getting up from a
chair on your own and needing someone to
help you. They are the difference
between carrying your own groceries and
being unable to, between playing on the
floor with your grandchildren and
watching from the couch. Every day you
give your muscles what they need. You
are protecting your freedom, your
dignity, and your quality of life. And
it is never too late.
I have seen people in their 80s and 90s
rebuild strength they thought was gone
forever. Your body is listening even
now. All it needs is a reason to
respond. Make your morning coffee the
reason. Add the nutrients, move your
body a little every day, and take one
small step today.

Constipation Relief: Stool Stuck in the Rectum? A Surgeon Explains What Helps 💡 | Dr. Jason Fung


Struggling with constipation, painful bowel movements, or the uncomfortable feeling that stool is stuck in your rectum? You are not alone. Constipation can affect comfort, confidence, sleep, and everyday quality of life, particularly as we grow older. There are moments in medicine that
nobody warns you about. Moments where
something that sounds minor, something
you might brush off as just a bad day,
turns out to be far more serious than
anyone imagined. And today I want to
talk about one of those moments because
in emergency medicine, I have seen
patients come in embarrassed,
uncomfortable, and genuinely suffering
from something that could have been
prevented weeks earlier if only someone
had told them what I am about to tell
you. I am Dr. Jason. I work in emergency
medicine in the United States. And
before you click away thinking this
topic does not apply to you, I want you
to stay with me for just 60 seconds
because what I am going to share today
is something that affects millions of
people silently. Something most people
are too embarrassed to Google and
something that a colorectal surgeon
colleague of mine recently broke down
for me in a way that genuinely changed
how I think about digestive health. If
you find this kind of real, honest
medical content valuable, I would love
for you to subscribe to this channel
right now. We do not do click bait here.
We do doctor level education, plain
language, no nonsense. Hit that
subscribe button and let us get into
this. So, stool stuck in the rectum,
fecal impaction. Even saying the words
out loud feels uncomfortable for most
people. But here is the thing,
discomfort with words is exactly why
this condition gets worse before anyone
does anything about it. People wait.
They hope it resolves on its own. They
drink a glass of water, maybe take a
laxative from the pharmacy shelf, and
then wait some more. And the clock keeps
ticking. Here is what is actually
happening inside your body when stool
becomes impacted in the rectum. The
rectum is the final holding chamber of
your digestive system. It sits just
above the anus and its job is to
temporarily store stool until your body
signals that it is ready to expel it.
Under normal conditions, this process is
elegant and automatic. But, when stool
sits in the rectum for too long,
something goes wrong at a cellular and
mechanical level. Water continues to be
absorbed from that stool. The longer it
stays, the harder, drier, and more
compacted it becomes. And here is where
things get interesting. Once that stool
reaches a certain density, the normal
muscular contractions of your colon,
those gentle waves that push everything
forward, can no longer move it. The
system stalls. And what was once a
manageable situation becomes a genuine
medical emergency if left unaddressed.
The rectum begins to stretch. That
stretch activates stretch receptors in
the wall of the rectum. Those receptors
send signals to your brain that you need
to go. So, you feel the urge, you go to
the bathroom, you sit there, nothing
happens or almost nothing. Maybe a small
amount of liquid stool seeps around the
impacted mass. And this is one of the
most dangerous and misunderstood signs
in this entire condition. Liquid stool
leaking around a solid impaction is not
diarrhea. It is paradoxical diarrhea. It
looks like a stomach bug. It looks like
a gut infection. And so, people treat it
like one. They take antidiarrheal
medication, and they make everything
dramatically worse. That is the part
most people miss. If you or someone you
love is experiencing what seems like
diarrhea, but also has not had a proper
bowel movement in days, that pattern
deserves immediate medical attention. Do
not treat it at home with
over-the-counter antidiarrheal drugs
without first confirming what is
actually happening. I want to say that
clearly, and I say it not to scare you,
but to give you the knowledge to act
correctly. Now, who is most at risk
here? The picture is broader than most
people think. Yes, older adults are
disproportionately affected. The
muscular contractions of the colon
naturally weaken with age, mobility
decreases, hydration often suffers,
fiber intake drops, medications like
opioid painkillers, certain
antidepressants, iron supplements, and
calcium channel blockers all slow gut
motility significantly. But, younger
people are not immune. Long periods of
immobility, dehydration from illness,
neglecting the to go repeatedly over
time, low-fiber diets, and certain
neurological conditions can all set the
stage for impaction regardless of age.
And here is a behavioral pattern I want
you to think about. How many times in
your life have you felt the urge to use
the bathroom and suppressed it because
you were in a meeting or on a trip or
just somewhere inconvenient?
Your body gives you a window. That
window is real. When you ignore it
repeatedly, you train your rectum to
stop sending the signals as urgently.
Over time, the threshold changes. Stool
stays longer. Drying begins. The cycle
builds quietly over months and years
before it becomes an acute crisis. Let
us talk about the one teaspoon that is
mentioned in the title because this is
where the science gets genuinely
fascinating and where my colorectal
surgeon colleague absolutely floored me
in conversation. What we are talking
about is something that has been used in
clinical medicine for decades, something
low-risk, widely available, and backed
by actual physiological mechanism. We
are talking about olive oil,
specifically around 1 tsp of
extra-virgin olive oil taken orally,
ideally first thing in the morning on an
empty stomach. Now, before I explain why
this works, let me be absolutely clear
about something. Olive oil is not a
treatment for severe or complete fecal
impaction. If you are having significant
pain, you cannot pass stool at all, your
abdomen is distended, or you have any
signs of obstruction, you need to go to
an emergency room, full stop. What we
are discussing here is the role of olive
oil in supporting rectal motility,
softening stool, and stimulating natural
bowel movement in cases of early or mild
constipation and sluggish rectal
evacuation. This is not a miracle. It is
a mechanism. Here is the physiology.
Olive oil is rich in oleic acid, a
monounsaturated fatty acid. When oleic
acid reaches the small intestine, it
triggers the release of something called
cholecystokinin, a gut hormone that
stimulates contraction of the
gallbladder and the secretion of
digestive enzymes. But, it also has a
direct effect on gut motility. It
essentially tells the intestinal tract
to move. On top of that, olive oil has a
lubricating effect on the intestinal
wall. It reduces friction. It makes it
easier for stool to slide through and
out. And one key study published in the
Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and
Dietetics found that olive oil was
comparably effective to mineral oil for
managing constipation in dialysis
patients, a population where
constipation is both common and
difficult to treat. 1 tsp first thing in
the morning, empty stomach. That small
act can be the difference between a
bowel movement happening within 30 to 60
minutes and a day of discomfort and
frustration.
It is not dramatic. It is not a shock to
your system. It is a gentle biochemical
nudge that works with your body's own
mechanisms, but it only works in the
right context and it is not the only
piece of this conversation. Cuz the
bigger picture here is about rectal
health as a daily practice, not an
emergency response. Fiber is
foundational, and here is where most
people get it wrong. They hear fiber and
they think bran cereal. They add a
little bit of fiber to their diet no
change and they give up. But, fiber has
two forms and both matter. Soluble
fiber, found in oats, apples, flaxseed,
and legumes, absorbs water and forms a
gel that slows digestion and softens
stool. Insoluble fiber, found in whole
grains, vegetables, and wheat bran, adds
bulk and speeds transit time through the
colon. You need both and the amount
matters. The average American gets
somewhere around 15 g of fiber per adult
and why the recommended minimum is 25 to
38 g depending on age and sex. That gap
is not a small statistical difference.
That gap is a daily driver of
constipation across millions of people.
Hydration is the second piece and this
one is criminally under estimated. Fiber
without adequate water can actually make
constipation worse. Think of fiber as a
sponge. Without water, it does not work.
It sits in your colon dry and adds to
the problem rather than solving it. You
need enough fluid for that fiber to do
its job. For most adults, that means
somewhere between six and eight glasses
of water per day as a baseline. More if
you are active, in a hot climate, or
consuming significant amounts of salt or
caffeine. Movement is the third piece.
Your colon has a direct relationship
with your body's physical activity.
Walking in particular stimulates
something called the gastrocolic reflex,
which is the same reflex that makes you
feel the urge to use the bathroom after
a meal. When you move your body, you
move your gut. People who are sedentary
have consistently slower colonic transit
times. Even a 20-minute walk after meals
can meaningfully reduce constipation
risk over time. And then there is the
question of position. This one surprises
people. The human rectum and anus are
not perfectly aligned when you are
seated in a modern toilet position. The
puborectalis muscle forms a kind of kink
in the anorectal canal when you are
seated upright. This is a natural design
feature that maintains continence,
meaning it helps you not have accidents.
But that same kink makes full evacuation
harder. When you squat or use a small
footstool to raise your knees above your
hips, that muscle relaxes. The anorectal
angle straightens and stool passes with
significantly less strain. This is not
folk medicine. This is anatomy and it is
supported by studies showing reduced
straining, less time on the toilet, and
more complete evacuation with a
squatting posture. I have patients who
have struggled with incomplete
evacuation for years, who feel like they
never quite finish, who spend more time
in the bathroom than they should. And
when I ask them about their toilet
posture, they have never once considered
it. A $6 footstool from a pharmacy can
genuinely change that experience. We are
at the middle of this video and I want
to pause and say something. If you are
getting value from this kind of detailed
science-backed medical content, please
subscribe to this channel. Share this
video with someone in your life who
deals with constipation silently because
that person exists in almost every
family and they deserve real
information, not shame and silence. Now,
let us talk about warning signs because
not all constipation is equal and part
of what I want you to take from this
video is the ability to distinguish
between something you can manage at home
and something that needs professional
evaluation. If you have not had a bowel
movement in more than 3 days and all of
oil, hydration, fiber, and movement are
not helping, call your doctor. If you
are experiencing significant abdominal
pain or cramping alongside the
constipation, do not wait. That level of
discomfort warrants evaluation. If you
notice blood in your stool, even a small
amount, even if you think it is just
hemorrhoids, mention it to a doctor.
Blood is always worth evaluating in the
context of a change in bowel habits. If
you are experiencing a significant and
unexplained change in your normal bowel
pattern, meaning you are someone who has
always been regular and suddenly find
yourself chronically constipated, that
is a conversation to have with your
health care provider.
Changes in bowel habit are new,
persistent, or accompanied by weight
loss, fatigue, or abdominal bloating
should be investigated. This is not
meant to alarm you. It is meant to give
you the knowledge to advocate for
yourself. Colorectal surgeons and
gastroenterologists are not people you
should be embarrassed to see. The
colorectal surgeon I spoke with recently
described it simply. He said that the
patients who suffer most from impaction
and chronic constipation are the ones
who waited too long to talk to someone
because they were embarrassed. And he
said that in his entire career, he has
never once judged a patient for a bowel
complaint. What he has seen is people
who suffered unnecessarily for months or
years because they assumed the
conversation would be awkward.
Let that land for a moment. The
practical summary here is this: Take 1
tsp of extra virgin olive oil in the
morning on an empty stomach. Eat both
soluble and insoluble fiber across your
meals. Drink enough water to give that
fiber the medium it needs to work. Walk
after meals. Use a footstool to optimize
your evacuation posture. Respond to the
urge when it comes. Do not suppress it
repeatedly. And if something feels
wrong, persistent, painful, or unusual,
talk to a doctor.
Not next month, soon. Fecal impaction is
not a punchline. It is not a minor
inconvenience. Left untreated, severe
impaction can cause rectal tears,
pressure ulcers, bowel obstruction, and
in the most extreme cases, a condition
called stercoral perforation, where the
pressure of impacted stool actually
perforates the bowel wall. That is a
surgical emergency with a high mortality
rate. And it almost always began as
something manageable that was ignored
for too long. I want you to take this
video seriously, not because I want to
frighten you, but because I genuinely
believe that the gap between a life with
easy, comfortable digestion, and a life
defined by chronic constipation,
discomfort, and eventual crisis is
smaller than most people think. And

🔥 What if one simple food could help you take a smarter approach to stubborn belly fat after 60?** As we age, changes in muscle mass, insulin sensitivity, appetite, and activity levels can make maintaining a healthy waistline more challenging. In this educational video, we explore the science behind a potentially helpful food choice, how nutrition influences metabolism, and why sustainable lifestyle habits matter more than miracle promises. Inspired by discussions of metabolic health and fasting associated with Dr. Jason Fung, this video examines practical strategies for adults over 60 who want to support healthier body composition.

Let me ask you something, and I want you
to be completely honest with yourself.
Have you noticed that even when you eat
less, even when you go for walks, even
when you try to do everything right,
that belly fat just will not move? You
wake up in the morning, look in the
mirror, and wonder what happened. You
used to be able to drop a few pounds
just by cutting back on bread for a
week. Now, it feels like your body has
completely stopped listening to you,
like it has its own agenda. And no
matter what you do, that stubborn,
frustrating belly fat stays exactly
where it is, or worse, it keeps growing.
I hear this from patients every single
day, and every single day I tell them
the same thing. You are not lazy, you're
not broken, and this is absolutely not
your fault. Here is what nobody is
telling you, and what I have spent over
20 years as a physician trying to help
people understand. After 60, your body
undergoes a dramatic and largely
invisible set of changes. Cortisol
rises, estrogen and testosterone fall,
your gut microbiome shifts, your liver
becomes less efficient, and your fat
cells, particularly the dangerous kind
that live deep inside your belly,
wrapped around your organs called
visceral fat, they become almost
completely resistant to traditional
dieting and calorie restriction. You can
starve yourself, and that fat will stay.
Your body is protecting it. But here is
the part that changes everything. There
are nine specific foods, ordinary,
inexpensive foods that you can find at
any grocery store, that have been shown
in peer-reviewed clinical research to
directly attack the biological
mechanisms that create and sustain
visceral fat. Not by starving you, not
by making you miserable, but by changing
the internal chemistry of your body at
the hormonal, inflammatory, and
metabolic level. I am Dr. Jason Fung,
and in the next few minutes, I am going
to walk you through every single one of
those foods, explain exactly why each
one works, and tell you precisely how to
use them. Stay with me because what I
share with you today could genuinely
change your health, your energy, and
your life. Before we get into the list,
I want to ask you one quick favor. If
you are finding this information
valuable, and I promise you it only gets
better from here, please take one single
second right now and hit the subscribe
button below this video.
One tap, that is all. I release a new
video every single week, all of it
designed specifically for people over
60, all of it completely free, all of it
based on real science. No fads, no
supplements I am trying to sell you,
just honest information that your body
deserves. And while you are down there,
leave me a comment. Tell me what city or
country you are watching from. I read
every comment personally, and I am
always moved by how far this community
reaches.
Whether you are in Toronto or Tokyo, in
London or Lagos, in a small town in
rural America or a bustling city in
India, I want to know you are here. Drop
your location below. It takes 2 seconds,
and it means more than you know. Now,
let us talk about why belly fat after 60
is so fundamentally different and so
much harder to fight than belly fat at
any other stage of your life. Visceral
fat is not the fat you can see or pinch.
It is not the soft layer under your
skin. Visceral fat lives inside your
abdominal cavity. It surrounds your
liver, your pancreas, your intestines,
your heart. You cannot feel it.
Sometimes you cannot even see it. A
person can have dangerous levels of
visceral fat without appearing
dramatically overweight, and it is not
just cosmetic. This fat is metabolically
active. It functions almost like a
hostile organ working directly against
your health. Research published in the
Journal of the American Medical
Association has linked high visceral fat
levels to elevated risk of type 2
diabetes, cardiovascular disease,
stroke, Alzheimer's disease, and several
forms of cancer. So, why does visceral
fat become so much harder to lose after
60? Three reasons. The first is hormonal
decline. When estrogen and testosterone
drop, the body signals fat storage to
relocate to the abdomen. This is an
ancient survival mechanism. Your biology
believes central fat protects your
organs in times of famine. It does not
know you live in a modern world. It is
trying to protect you, and in doing so,
it is slowly harming you. The second
reason is chronic inflammation. Visceral
fat actively secretes inflammatory
proteins called cytokines, including
interleukin-6 and TNF alpha. These
cytokines make your cells resistant to
insulin, slow your metabolism, and make
the visceral fat itself harder to break
down. It is as if the fat has built its
own immune system. The third reason is
sarcopenia, the age-related loss of
muscle mass. After 60, most people lose
3 to 5% of their muscle per decade. Less
muscle means a slower resting
metabolism, and visceral fat actively
accelerates muscle loss. So, the more
visceral fat you carry, the slower your
metabolism, and the more visceral fat
accumulates. A biological trap. But,
every trap has a way out, and the exit
here is targeted nutrition. Let me show
you exactly what that looks like. Food
number one, avocado.
Avocado is one of the most powerful and
most underutilized foods available to
people over 60. It works through a
mechanism that most people have never
heard of. Avocado is extraordinarily
rich in oleic acid, a monounsaturated
fatty acid shown in multiple clinical
trials to reduce abdominal fat directly.
A landmark study at Penn State
University found that participants who
consumed one avocado per Dalton Y for 12
weeks experienced a measurable and
statistically significant reduction in
visceral fat compared to a control group
eating the same calories from other fat
sources. Oleic acid works by activating
a gene pathway that tells your liver and
muscle cells to use fat as fuel rather
than store it. This is a documented
molecular mechanism, not a theory.
Beyond oleic acid, avocado contains more
potassium than a banana, which reduces
the water retention and bloating that
often makes visceral fat look and feel
worse than it is. And its high soluble
fiber content feeds the gut bacteria
responsible for lowering systemic
inflammation, the same inflammation that
locks visceral fat in place. Half an
avocado per day is sufficient. Add it to
eggs in the morning or slice it into a
salad at lunch. It is that simple and
that effective. Food number two,
blueberries. If there is a single food I
recommend to every patient over 60 who
comes to me concerned about visceral
fat, it is the blueberry. Not because it
is trendy, but because the science is
genuinely remarkable. Blueberries are
among the richest dietary sources of
anthocyanins, a class of flavonoid
antioxidants studied extensively for
their effects on fat metabolism. A
University of Michigan study
demonstrated that animals fed a
blueberry-enriched diet accumulated
significantly less visceral fat than
control animals, even with identical
total caloric intake. The calories were
the same, the fat storage was
dramatically different. The only
variable was the blueberries. In human
studies, the mechanism operates through
two distinct pathways. First,
anthocyanins suppress fat cell
differentiation at the level of gene
expression, literally interfering with
your body's ability to create new fat
cells. Second, they dramatically reduce
circulating levels of interleukin-6 and
TNF-alpha, the exact inflammatory
cytokines that visceral fat uses to
sustain and protect itself. One cup of
blueberries per day is the therapeutic
threshold established in the research.
Fresh or frozen makes no difference
because the anthocyanin content is
equivalent in both forms. Add them to
yogurt, to oatmeal, or eat them plain.
Make this a daily non-negotiable. Food
number three, fatty fish, salmon,
sardines, mackerel, herring. These are
not just broadly healthy foods. They are
among the most targeted visceral fat
interventions available in the natural
food supply. Fatty fish are the richest
dietary source of long-chain omega-3
fatty acids, specifically EPA and DHA.
These omega-3s activate a protein called
adiponectin, which circulates through
your bloodstream and signals visceral
fat cells to release their stored energy
and allow themselves to be burned as
fuel. Low adiponectin levels are one of
the most consistent biological markers
of high visceral fat. Omega-3s raise
adiponectin, visceral fat falls.
Simultaneously, EPA and DHA are among
the most potent natural
anti-inflammatory
compounds known to nutritional science.
They directly suppress the cytokine
production that visceral fat relies on
for its own self-preservation. A study
published in the International Journal
of Obesity found that adults who consume
fatty fish twice per week lost
significantly more visceral fat over 12
weeks than participants eating the same
total calories without fatty fish with
no other dietary changes required. Two
to three servings per week is the
target. If fresh salmon is outside your
budget, canned sardines packed in olive
oil are equally effective and you are
combining two items from this very list
at the same time. Food number four,
green tea. Most people think of green
tea as a pleasant, mildly healthy drink,
a gentle antioxidant, something nice in
the morning. Then they see the clinical
data and that perception changes
completely. Green tea contains a
specific catechin called EGCG, which
stands for epigallocatechin
gallate. EGCG is one one most
comprehensively studied natural
compounds in the scientific literature
on visceral fat reduction. A randomized
controlled trial published in the
American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
found that participants who consumed
green tea containing EGCG daily for 12
weeks lost an average of 17% more
visceral fat than the placebo group, not
total body fat. Specifically and
measurably visceral fat. The mechanism
is well understood. EGCG activates an
enzyme called AMPK, adenosine
monophosphate activated protein kinase,
which functions as a master metabolic
switch in your cells. When AMPK is
activated, your cells shift from fat
storage mode into fat burning mode, and
EGCG drives this process specifically in
visceral adipose tissue. Three cups of
warm green tea per day consumed without
sweetener. Give it 30 days. The results
will be measurable. Food number five,
cruciferous vegetables, broccoli,
cauliflower, brussels sprouts, cabbage,
kale. These vegetables share a
biochemical property that makes them
uniquely effective against one of the
most overlooked drivers of visceral fat
in people over 60, which is estrogen
imbalance. As we age, a process called
aromatization causes the body to convert
testosterone into estrogen in both men
and women. Visceral fat tissue is
particularly active in this conversion.
More visceral fat means more aromatase
enzyme activity, which means more
estrogen. Elevated estrogen drives
further visceral fat accumulation. The
cycle feeds itself and is almost never
discussed in conventional medicine.
Cruciferous vegetables contain a
compound called indole-3-carbinol,
which is converted in the digestive
process into diindolylmethane,
commonly known as DIM. DIM supports
healthy estrogen metabolism by guiding
excess estrogen toward a safer, less
potent metabolite rather than the form
that drives fat storage. It essentially
disrupts the hormonal environment that
visceral fat depends on to grow. One
serving of cruciferous vegetables per
day is sufficient to produce a
meaningful effect. Steam them, roast
them, eat them raw. It's the preparation
method matters far less than the
consistency of consumption. Food number
six, eggs. For decades, eggs were
unfairly and incorrectly vilified. The
science has since been thoroughly
reviewed and the consensus has shifted
dramatically. Eggs are not only safe for
the vast majority of adults over 60,
they are one of the most powerful
metabolic foods you can eat. The reason
is protein quality. Eggs contain all
nine essential amino acids in
proportions that match human metabolic
needs almost perfectly. Protein has a
high thermic effect, meaning your body
burns more calories digesting it than
fat or carbohydrates. It also suppresses
ghrelin, the hunger hormone that tends
to be elevated in seniors, and provides
the raw material your body needs to
maintain muscle mass and keep your
metabolism high enough to burn visceral
fat. Eggs are also one of the best
sources of choline, one of the most
commonly deficient nutrients in adults
over 60. Choline is essential for liver
function, and your liver is the primary
site of fat oxidation in your body. A
choline-deficient liver accumulates fat
rather than burning it. Two to three
eggs per day is appropriate for most
healthy adults. If your physician has
advised otherwise, follow their
guidance. But, if you have been avoiding
eggs over outdated cholesterol concerns,
the current science strongly supports
bringing them back. Food number seven,
garlic. Garlic has been used medicinally
for over 5,000 years across virtually
every culture on Earth. Modern molecular
biology is now revealing exactly why it
deserves that reputation. The active
compound in raw garlic is allicin, a
sulfur-containing
molecule that is released when garlic is
crushed or chopped and allowed to rest
before being consumed or cooked. Allicin
has been shown in multiple peer-reviewed
studies to reduce visceral fat
accumulation by suppressing the
expression of genes responsible for fat
cell formation and lipid storage. A 2011
clinical study demonstrated that garlic
supplementation produced significant
reductions in total body weight and
specifically in visceral fat without any
other dietary modification. The effect
was attributed primarily to allicin's
ability to reduce circulating insulin
levels and suppress the genetic
machinery of fat cell creation. Garlic
also meaningfully reduces cortisol, the
stress hormone that becomes chronically
elevated in many adults over 60, and
that is one of the most direct
biological drivers of abdominal fat
accumulation. When cortisol is
persistently high, your body locks fat
in the abdominal region as emergency
energy storage. Reducing cortisol helps
release that lock. Two to three fresh
cloves per Dalton why crush them, let
them rest 10 minutes before cooking to
maximize allicin release, and add them
to whatever you are already making. Food
number eight, legumes, lentils,
chickpeas, black beans, kidney beans,
white beans. This food category is among
the most powerful metabolic
interventions available in the entire
food supply, and it is dramatically
underutilized by people over 60.
Legumes have an exceptionally low
glycemic index, meaning they cause a
slow modest rise in blood glucose and a
proportionally small insulin response.
This matters enormously for visceral fat
because chronically elevated insulin is
one of the primary hormonal signals that
drives visceral fat storage. Every
significant insulin spike sends a clear
message to your body, store fat
centrally. Legumes help keep that signal
quiet hour after hour throughout the
day. Beyond glycemic control, legumes
are among the richest dietary sources of
resistant starch, a form of prebiotic
fiber that passes undigested into the
colon and feeds beneficial bacteria. The
diversity and health of your gut
microbiome has been directly linked in
multiple large human studies to visceral
fat levels. People with more diverse gut
bacteria consistently carry less
visceral fat entirely independent of
total caloric intake. One cup per day in
soups, stews, or salads, inexpensive,
filling, and remarkably effective. Food
number nine, extra virgin olive oil.
Extra virgin olive oil is the final food
on this list, and in many ways it is the
one that ties everything else together.
Olive oil is the foundational fat of the
Mediterranean dietary pattern, which has
been studied in more large-scale human
trials than virtually any other dietary
approach in the history of nutritional
science.
Its effects on cardiovascular health,
systemic inflammation, and visceral fat
are among the most robustly documented
findings in the literature. The compound
most responsible for olive oil's
anti-inflammatory power is called
oleocanthal. Oleocanthal inhibits the
same enzymatic pathway targeted by
ibuprofen, producing a powerful and
sustained anti-inflammatory effect that
directly undermines the environment
visceral fat needs to survive and
expand. The critical difference is that
oleocanthal does this without the
gastrointestinal risks associated with
long-term anti-inflammatory drug use,
which is a meaningful advantage for
adults over 60 who are often already
managing multiple medications. The
PREDIMED trial, one of the largest
nutrition studies ever conducted, found
that daily extra virgin olive oil
consumption produced measurably lower
visceral fat levels compared to low-fat
dietary controls alongside significantly
fewer cardiovascular events. Two
tablespoons per day over salads or
cooked vegetables. The distinction is
extra virgin, not light, not blended.
Refining strips away the oleocanthal and
polyphenols that make it work. Only
extra virgin delivers what the research
documents. Nine foods: avocado,
blueberries, fatty fish, green tea,
cruciferous vegetables, eggs, garlic,
legumes, extra virgin olive oil. Each
one works through a distinct and
documented biological mechanism
addressing visceral fat not as a simple
calorie problem, but as the hormonal,
inflammatory, and metabolic condition it
truly is in people over 60. Together,
they create a nutritional environment
where visceral fat cannot sustain
itself, where the signals that protect
and grow it are progressively weakened,
and where your metabolism and immune
system begin working with you instead of
against you. This is not a crash diet or
a deprivation protocol. It is nine
foods, most of which you can already
find in your kitchen, used with
intention and consistency. Here is your
one action step. of these nine foods and
commit to eating them every single day
for 30 days. Just three. Notice how your
energy changes, how your sleep improves,
how your clothing fits differently. Then
come back and tell me what happened. I
read every comment. If this video helped
you, share it with someone who needs it.
A spouse, a sibling, a parent. The
people in your life over 60 deserve this
information, and most will never hear it
in a standard doctor's appointment.

THIS 1 Overlooked Spice May Help Reduce Visceral Fat 🌶️🔥 | Dr Jason Fung
 

Could a simple spice in your kitchen support your journey toward a healthier waistline and better metabolic health? 🌶️ As we age, excess visceral fat—the fat stored deep inside the abdomen around vital organs—can become an important health concern. In this 16-minute educational video, we explore **chili pepper and capsaicin**, its naturally occurring active compound, and what scientific research reveals about its potential role in weight management, appetite regulation, energy expenditure, and metabolic health.

Many people over 60 struggle with stubborn belly fat, declining energy, and changes in metabolism. But lasting progress does not require miracle cures or extreme diets. Understanding how nutrition, physical activity, sleep, and insulin regulation work together can help you make more informed decisions. Research suggests capsaicin may offer modest weight-management benefits, but no spice has been proven to melt visceral fat faster than every diet. The goal is to understand the evidence and use it wisely.

subtitles.plaintext:
A 65-year-old patient walked into my
care with visceral fat levels so high
his organs were being crushed, liver
failing, insulin resistance through the
roof. Every diet he tried for 8 years,
nothing moved it. I told him to add one
specific spice to his meals daily, 2 g,
that is it. 10 weeks later his visceral
fat dropped 17%, his metabolic panel
reversed, his dietitian could not
explain it. I could because this spice
does something no diet on earth can do
alone. Right now, visceral fat is
wrapping around your organs like toxic
insulation. After 40, your body
preferentially stores fat around your
liver, kidneys, and intestines. That fat
is not passive. It is an active
endocrine organ pumping out inflammatory
cytokines driving insulin resistance,
spiking cortisol, accelerating every
disease that kills you after 60. And no
calorie deficit touches it because
visceral fat does not respond to
restriction.
It responds to specific biochemical
signals. This spice sends exactly those
signals. Here is what makes me furious
as a surgeon. I have opened abdomens
coated in visceral fat, organs drowning
in it, and these patients dieted,
exercised, starved themselves, did
everything they were told. A $270
billion weight loss industry sold them
meal plans designed to shrink
subcutaneous fat, the fat under your
skin. Visceral fat has different
receptors, different hormonal locks,
different rules entirely. Nobody
explained the difference because
explaining it eliminates the need for
their products. This spice activates
AMPK, the enzyme that unlocks visceral
fat cells specifically. It suppresses
lipogenesis in the liver, reduces
inflammatory markers that command your
body to store abdominal fat. Clinical
trials measured visceral fat reduction
that outperformed standard dietary
intervention alone. Published,
replicated, completely overlooked. You
cut calories, walk daily, avoided sugar,
and your belly never changed because you
were fighting the wrong fat with the
wrong weapon. In this video, we will
reveal exactly which spice melts
visceral fat and the science behind why
it works. The mechanism behind it will
change everything you thought about
belly fat. References are in the
description. How old and where are you
watching from? Drop it below. I read
every comment. I reply personally. Now,
let us start with why visceral fat
ignores every traditional diet and what
this single spice triggers inside your
fat cells from the very first dose.
Number five, black pepper. Most people
think of black pepper as nothing more
than a table seasoning. You shake it on
your eggs, you grind it over your steak,
and you never think about it again. But,
black pepper contains a bio-active
compound
called piperine. And piperine is one of
the most underestimated fat-fighting
molecules in the entire spice world. A
study published in the Journal of
Agricultural and Food Chemistry found
that piperine directly interferes with
the formation of new fat cells through a
process called adipogenesis.
In simple terms,
your body is constantly creating new fat
cells, especially when you eat processed
foods and sugars. Piperine steps in and
disrupts that process at the genetic
level. It actually down-regulates the
genes responsible for fat cell creation.
The researchers found that piperine
reduced fat cell formation by a
significant margin in laboratory models.
And this was not at some impossibly high
dose. Another study from the Indian
Journal of Pharmacology tested piperine
on subjects with metabolic issues and
found that daily supplementation led to
meaningful reductions in total
cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and
triglyceride levels over a period of
just 6 weeks. Triglycerides are directly
linked to visceral fat accumulation. So,
when your triglycerides drop, it is a
strong indicator that your visceral fat
stores are shrinking. But, here's the
part that makes black pepper truly
special and why it earned a spot on this
list. Piperine dramatically increases
the bioavailability of other nutrients
and compounds. Bioavailability just
means how much of a substance your body
can actually absorb and use. For
example, turmeric on its own has very
poor absorption. Your body struggles to
use it. But, when you add black pepper,
piperine increases the absorption of
turmeric's active compound by up to
2,000%. That is not a small boost. That
is the difference between a spice doing
almost nothing and a spice completely
transforming your metabolism. So, black
pepper works in two powerful ways.
First, it fights fat on its own by
blocking new fat cell creation and
lowering lipid levels. Second, it
supercharges the effects of every other
spice on this list. The best way to use
black pepper is freshly ground, not the
pre-ground stuff that has been sitting
in a container for months losing its
potency. You want to crack whole
peppercorns right before you use them
because piperine degrades over time when
exposed to air and light. Aim for about
half a teaspoon per day spread across
your meals. Add it to soups, salads,
cooked vegetables, and smoothies. And
always always pair it with the other
spices on this list because that
combination effect is where the real
magic happens. Fresh ground black pepper
added to warm dishes at the end of
cooking preserves the piperine content
best. Do not boil it for extended
periods because high sustained heat
breaks down the compound. A quick stir
into finished dishes is the ideal method
to get maximum benefit from every single
grain. Now, let us move to a spice that
brings serious heat and even more
serious science. Number four, ginger.
Ginger has been used in traditional
medicine for thousands of years, but
modern science is only now catching up
to what ancient healers seem to already
know. This root contains powerful
compounds called gingerols and shogaols,
and these molecules have a direct impact
on how your body stores and burns fat. A
major meta-analysis published in the
Annals of the New York Academy of
Sciences reviewed the 14th of September
air eight studies on ginger and body
weight. The results were striking.
Participants who consumed ginger daily
experienced significant reductions in
body weight, waist-to-hip ratio, and
fasting blood sugar levels compared to
those who did not. The waist-to-hip
ratio finding is particularly important
here because that measurement is a
direct indicator of visceral fat. When
your waist-to-hip ratio drops, it means
the fat around your internal organs is
shrinking. Another landmark study
published in the European Journal of
Nutrition found that ginger
supplementation increased the thermic
effect of food by approximately 43
calories per minute meal. That might not
sound like much, but across three meals
a day over 365 days, that adds up to
roughly 47,000 extra calories burned per
year just from adding ginger. The
thermic effect of food refers to the
energy your body uses to digest, absorb,
and process nutrients. Ginger
essentially turns up the dial on your
internal furnace. But the visceral fat
connection goes even deeper than
thermogenesis. A 2019 study in the
journal Phytotherapy Research found that
ginger supplementation for 12 weeks
significantly reduced levels of
C-reactive protein, which is one of the
primary markers of the chronic
inflammation that visceral fat causes.
When inflammation drops, your body
becomes more efficient at burning stored
fat, particularly the deep abdominal fat
that is hardest to lose. It creates a
positive cycle where less inflammation
leads to more fat burning, which leads
to even less inflammation. The best way
to consume ginger for fat loss is as
fresh ginger root, not the dried powder,
although the powder still offers
benefits. Take a piece of fresh ginger
about the size of your thumb, peel it
and slice it thinly. Then steep it in
hot water for 10 to 15 minutes to make a
concentrated ginger tea. Drinking this
first thing in the morning on an empty
stomach appears to be the most effective
timing based on the research. The hot
water extracts the gingerols efficiently
and consuming it before food means the
compounds are rapidly absorbed without
competition from other nutrients. You
can also grate fresh ginger directly
into stir-fries, soups, and salad
dressings. Aim for about 2 g of fresh
ginger per Dalton why, which is roughly
1 tsp of grated root. Consistency is the
key here. The studies that showed the
best results were the ones where
participants consumed ginger every
single day without skipping. It is the
daily habit that produces the
compounding effect over weeks and
months. But, the next spice takes the
fat burning conversation to a completely
different level. Number three, turmeric.
Turmeric is the golden spice that has
taken the health world by storm in
recent years and for very good reason.
It's active compound is called curcumin,
and the research on curcumin and
visceral fat is genuinely remarkable. A
randomized control trial published in
the European Review for Medical and
Pharmacological Sciences studied 44
people who were struggling to lose
weight. They gave one group curcumin
supplements and the other group a
placebo for 30 days. The curcumin group
experienced a 4.91%
increase in weight loss, an 8.43%
increase in body fat reduction, and a
236%
further reduction in BMI compared to
placebo in just 1 month. Those are the
kind of numbers that make researchers
sit up and pay attention. The reason
curcumin is so effective against
visceral fat specifically comes down to
its extraordinary anti-inflammatory
power.
Visceral fat is not just sitting there
passively. It's an active endocrine
organ that pumps out inflammatory
molecules called cytokines. These
cytokines tell your body to store even
more fat, create insulin resistance, and
damage your blood vessels. Curcumin
directly suppresses the production of
these inflammatory cytokines. A study in
the journal BioFactors showed that
curcumin inhibits the NF-κB pathway,
which is the master switch of
inflammation in the body. When you turn
down that switch, your body stops
getting the signal to keep packing on
visceral fat. Another study published in
the journal Nutrition Research found
that curcumin supplementation reduced
serum triglycerides by 25%
in overweight individuals over 12 weeks.
Remember, high triglycerides are one of
the hallmark signs of excess visceral
fat. But here is the critical detail
most people get wrong about turmeric.
Curcumin has notoriously poor
bioavailability on its own. Your liver
processes it so quickly that very little
reaches your bloodstream. This is
exactly where black pepper from our
number five spot becomes essential.
Combining turmeric with black pepper
increases curcumin absorption by that
2000% we discussed earlier. You also
want to consume turmeric with some form
of fat because curcumin is fat soluble,
meaning it dissolves in fat rather than
water. The best preparation method is
what is called golden milk. Warm up a
cup of full-fat coconut milk or regular
whole milk. Add 1 tsp of turmeric
powder. Add a generous pinch of freshly
ground black pepper, stir it well, and
drink about 30 minutes before your
evening meal. The fat in the milk helps
your body absorb the curcumin. The
piperine from the pepper prevents your
liver from clearing it too fast. And the
evening timing works well because your
body does much of its metabolic repair
and fat processing during sleep. Aim for
at least 500 mgs of curcumin daily to
match the dosages used in clinical
studies. Consistency over weeks is what
produces the visible changes in waist
circumference and inflammatory markers.
And now we arrive at a spice that
directly targets your blood sugar, which
is the hidden key to visceral fat.
Number two, cinnamon. Cinnamon is
arguably the most delicious spice on
this list, and the science behind its
effect on visceral fat is absolutely
fascinating. The connection comes
through insulin, the hormone that
controls your blood sugar. When you eat
food, especially carbohydrates, your
blood sugar rises and your pancreas
releases insulin to bring it back down.
Insulin's job is to shuttle that sugar
into your cells for energy. But here is
the problem. When you have excess
visceral fat, your cells become
resistant to insulin. They stop
listening to the signal. So your
pancreas pumps out more and more insulin
to compensate. And chronically high
insulin levels tell your body to store
even more fat, especially around your
organs. It is a vicious cycle and
cinnamon appears to break it. A
groundbreaking study published in
Diabetes Care, one of the most respected
journals in the field, studied 60 people
with type 2 diabetes. They gave
participants either 1, 3, or 6 g of
cinnamon per adult and Y for 40 days.
All three groups showed remarkable
improvements. Fasting blood sugar
dropped by 18 to 29%. Total cholesterol
fell by 12 to 26%.
LDL cholesterol dropped by 7 to 27%.
And triglycerides decreased by 23 to
30%. These numbers are extraordinary for
a simple kitchen spice. The mechanism
works because cinnamon contains a
compound called methylhydroxychalcone
polymer, which mimics insulin in the
body. It helps your cells absorb sugar
from the blood without needing as much
actual insulin. Lower insulin means your
body gets the signal to start burning
stored fat instead of creating more of
it. A separate study published in the
Journal of the International Society of
Sports Nutrition found that cinnamon
supplementation for 12 weeks led to
significant reductions in body fat
percentage even without dietary changes.
Participants lost measurable amounts of
fat mass while maintaining their lean
muscle tissue. Now, the type of cinnamon
you use matters enormously. There are
two main types. Cassia cinnamon is the
common variety found in most grocery
stores. Ceylon cinnamon, sometimes
called true cinnamon, is the preferred
choice for daily consumption. Cassia
contains higher levels of a compound
called coumarin, which can stress your
liver if consumed in large daily doses
over time. Ceylon cinnamon has
significantly less coumarin and is safer
for consistent daily use. The ideal
daily dose based on the research is
about 1 to 2 tsp per day. Add it to your
morning coffee or tea, sprinkle it on
oatmeal or yogurt, blend it into
smoothies. You can also make a simple
cinnamon water by stirring a teaspoon
into warm water and drinking it before
meals to help blunt the blood sugar
spike from your food. The pre-meal
timing is particularly effective because
it gives the active compounds time to
start working before the glucose from
your meal hits your bloodstream. Some
people also add a cinnamon stick to a
water bottle and sip throughout the day
for a steady low-dose delivery method,
but nothing on this list compares to
what I am about to show you at number
one. Number one, cumin. This is the
spice that absolutely stunned the
research community, and when you see the
numbers, you will understand why it
claimed the top spot on this list.
Cumin, that humble brownish spice
sitting in your cabinet that you
probably only associate with chili or
tacos, turns out to be one of the most
potent natural visceral fat fighters
ever studied.

Don't Dye Your Hair Yet! — THIS 1 Vitamin May Help Naturally After 60 | Dr. Jason Fung
 

Have you ever looked in the mirror and wondered whether your gray hair is simply a sign of aging—or a signal that your body needs attention? Before reaching for another bottle of hair dye, discover the science behind hair pigmentation, vitamin B12, and healthy aging. In this educational 21-minute video, we explore how nutritional deficiencies may contribute to changes in hair color, why some people experience premature graying, and what scientific research actually says about restoring natural pigmentation after 60. Inspired by conversations about metabolic health and longevity associated with Dr. Jason Fung, this video separates evidence from exaggerated promises.


TIMESTAMPS:
00:00 🌿 Introduction: Think Before You Dye Your Hair
01:15 🧬 Why Hair Turns Gray as We Age
03:20 💊 Vitamin B12: What Science Reveals
05:30 🔬 The Connection Between Nutritional Deficiency and Hair Color
07:40 🥚 Foods That Support Healthy Hair
09:45 🩸 Signs of Possible Vitamin B12 Deficiency
11:40 🦋 Thyroid Health and Hair Changes
13:30 🥗 Nutrition, Metabolic Health, and Aging
15:20 🚫 Common Myths About Reversing Gray Hair
17:00 🩺 When to Consider Blood Tests and Medical Advice
18:40 🌱 Healthy Habits for Hair and Longevity
20:00 ❤️ Final Takeaways: Aging With Confidence
21:00 ✅ Conclusion


KEYWORDS:
vitamin for gray hair, reverse gray hair naturally, vitamin B12 for hair, gray hair after 60, natural hair pigmentation, healthy aging tips, Dr Jason Fung health, premature graying causes, vitamin deficiency and gray hair, hair health after 60, anti-aging nutrition, foods for healthy hair, oxidative stress and aging, thyroid health and hair, senior wellness, longevity tips, nutritional deficiencies, natural hair care, healthy aging after 60, science-based health advice

Consult a qualified healthcare professional before taking supplements or changing your treatment plan. Do not stop prescribed medication or delay medical evaluation based on this video.
