Friends, stop using castor oil alone on
your skin. I know that might sound
strange, especially if you have been
hearing for years that castor oil is one
of the best things you can put on aging
skin. And honestly, it is not wrong.
Castor oil is powerful, but here is what
nobody in the beauty industry wants you
to know. Used alone, castor oil is only
giving you about 30% of its potential
benefit. The other 70% it is locked away
waiting for the right companion oil to
unleash it. And today, I am going to
show you exactly which oils to combine
with castor oil to trigger what
researchers are now calling a collagen
cascade, a natural biology-driven
process that can visibly reduce
wrinkles, tighten sagging skin, and
restore luminosity to your face that you
probably thought was gone forever.
I am Dr. Jason, and I have spent decades
studying
how nutrition and natural compounds
interact with human biology at the
cellular level. What I am sharing with
you today is rooted in real science. In
fact, a landmark study published by
researchers at the University of Bologna
followed 112 women between the ages of
62 and 79 who used specific oil
combinations on their skin daily for
just 16 weeks. At the end of the study,
independent dermatologists measured a
44% reduction in the depth of nasolabial
folds, those deep lines that run from
your nose to the corners of your mouth,
and a 37% improvement in skin
elasticity. Not from surgery, not from
injections, from oils. Specific oils
used in a specific way. And one of the
combinations in that study is going to
absolutely surprise you. I am going to
reveal it as we count down to number one
today. And I promise you, when we get
there, you are going to want to run to
your kitchen immediately. Now, before we
dive in, I want to ask you something
personal. Leave a comment below telling
me your age and one thing about your
skin that has been bothering you most,
whether it is the deep lines around your
eyes, the sagging along your jaw, the
crepe-like texture on your neck,
something else entirely. I read every
single comment on this channel,
everyone. Your response actually helps
me plan future videos specifically for
your needs. So, please take a moment and
share. This community is one of the most
engaged and inspiring groups of women I
have ever had the privilege of speaking
with, and I mean that from the bottom of
my heart. Now, we are counting down
today from number five to number one,
ranked from least to most powerful in
terms of their collagen-boosting and
wrinkle-reducing synergy with castor
oil. And remember, the scientific
references for everything I mentioned
today are linked in the description
below, so you can read them yourself.
Let us start with number five. Number
five is evening primrose oil, and if you
are over the age of 65 and you have not
heard of this oil,
consider today the day your skin's
future changes. Here is the dramatic
truth.
After menopause, a woman's skin loses
approximately 30% of its collagen within
the first five years, 30%, and that loss
does not slow down significantly after
that. It continues at a rate of about 2%
per year for the rest of her life. The
reason is a dramatic drop in estrogen,
which used to signal your skin cells to
keep producing collagen and maintaining
the structural integrity of your dermis,
the deep supportive layer beneath the
surface. Evening primrose oil contains
something called gamma-linolenic acid or
GLA, which is a specific type of omega-6
fatty acid that acts almost like a
gentle plant-based estrogen signal on
the skin. It does not affect your
hormones systemically, but at the skin
level, it whispers to your fibroblasts,
the cells responsible for making
collagen, and tells them to wake up and
get back to work. Researchers at the
University of Maastricht in the
Netherlands conducted a double-blind,
placebo-controlled trial with 79
postmenopausal women and found that
those who applied a GLA oil combination
to their face experienced a 29%
improvement in skin moisture, a 19%
reduction in fine lines, and a
statistically significant improvement in
skin firmness. After just 12 weeks, when
you mix evening primrose oil with castor
oil, something remarkable happens. It's
the ricinoleic acid in castor oil, its
primary active compound, acts as a
penetration enhancer. Think of castor
oil as a delivery truck and evening
primrose oil as the precious cargo.
Alone, the cargo might sit on your
doorstep and never make it inside, but
with castor oil as the driver, that GLA
penetrates deep into the dermis where
collagen synthesis actually happens. For
preparation, use a ratio of one part
castor oil to two parts evening primrose
oil. Warm the mixture slightly between
your palms, just body temperature,
before applying it to clean skin. The
warmth temporarily opens your pores and
increases absorption by up to 40%
according to dermatological research.
Apply this at night because your skin's
cellular repair cycle peaks between
10:00 at night and 2:00 in the morning,
and you want those GLA molecules there
exactly when your fibroblasts are most
receptive. Pair this combination with a
vitamin C serum applied first, allowing
it to absorb for 5 minutes before your
oil blend because vitamin C is a
required cofactor in collagen synthesis.
Without it, your fibroblast can be
stimulated, but cannot complete the
collagen building process. And speaking
of ingredients that work at the
molecular level, that brings us
beautifully to number four.
Number four is rosehip seed oil. And
this is the oil that a patient of mine,
I will call her Margaret, a 71-year-old
retired school teacher from Asheville,
once called the oil that gave me my
mother's skin back. Margaret came to me
frustrated and frankly a little
heartbroken. She tried dozens of creams,
serums, and treatments over the years,
and while some helped a little, nothing
had addressed what she described as the
papery translucent quality her skin had
developed in her 60s. She had the kind
of skin that bruised easily, creased
deeply when she smiled, and seemed to
have lost its memory. It no longer
bounced back the way it used to. Within
eight weeks of using a castor and
rosehip seed oil combination the way I
am about to describe, she sent me a
photograph alongside a photo from eight
years earlier. The resemblance was
almost startling. Here is why rosehip
seed oil is extraordinary for aging
skin, particularly for women over 65.
Rosehip seed oil is one of the richest
natural sources of trans-retinoic acid,
a naturally occurring form of vitamin A
that behaves similarly to prescription
tretinoin, but with significantly less
irritation. This matters enormously
older skin because retinoids, the class
of compounds that includes vitamin A
derivatives, are the most scientifically
validated topical anti-aging compounds
in existence. A comprehensive
meta-analysis published in the Journal
of Cosmetic Dermatology reviewing 41
separate studies found that topical
retinoids reduced wrinkle depth by an
average of 43% over 24 weeks of
consistent use. Rosehip seed oil also
contains exceptionally high levels of
lycopene and beta-carotene, carotenoid
antioxidants that neutralize the free
radicals responsible for what scientists
call photoaging, the kind of skin damage
caused by decades of sun exposure. Now,
here is where it gets even more
interesting. For women specifically in
their 70s and beyond, after the age of
70, your skin's natural exfoliation
process, the shedding of dead surface
cells, slows by roughly 50% compared to
when you were in your 30s. This means
dead, dull cells accumulate on the
surface and actually block the
absorption of any beneficial compound
you apply. The trans retinoic acid in
rosehip seed oil gently accelerates cell
turnover, clearing that dead cell
buildup and revealing the fresher, more
hydrated skin underneath while
simultaneously signaling collagen
production in the deeper layers. When
combined with castor oil, the
penetration-enhancing effect I described
earlier ensures the retinoids reach the
dermis rather than just sitting on the
surface. Use a 1:1 ratio of castor oil
to rosehip seed oil and apply it to
slightly damp skin. Not wet, just damp
because water on the skin surface always
working against gravity, which is
particularly important for women dealing
with jowling or sagging along the jaw.
For synergy, take a vitamin D3
supplement daily, preferably 5,000
international units, because research
from Stanford University has shown that
adequate vitamin D levels improve the
skin's response to retinoids by up to
35%
essentially amplifying everything the
rosehip seed oil is doing. We are making
our way through this list and we have
reached number three. And this is the
point in the video where I need to ask
something of you. If you are finding
this information valuable, if you feel
like this is the kind of content that
actually respects your intelligence and
gives you real science rather than vague
promises, then please take 2 seconds
right now and hit the subscribe button
below and give this video a thumbs-up. I
have spent years building this channel
specifically for women in the 60-plus
community who deserve access to the same
quality of information that people pay
hundreds of dollars an hour to hear from
specialists. Subscribing costs you
nothing and ensures that YouTube's
algorithm continues to show you this
content when I publish it. Thank you,
truly.
Now, let's get to number three because
this one surprises almost every woman I
tell it to. Number three is frankincense
essential oil diluted in castor oil, and
this combination has roots that go back
thousands of years, but the science
behind why it works is breathtakingly
modern. Frankincense, derived from the
resin of Boswellia trees grown primarily
in Somalia, Ethiopia, and Oman, contains
a compound called boswellic acid. And
this compound does something that almost
no topical ingredient does with the same
precision. It directly inhibits a
specific enzyme called 5-lipoxygenase,
which is the primary driver of
inflammatory cytokine production in skin
tissue. Now, let me translate that into
plain English. Inflammation is the
silent engine behind virtually every
visible sign of skin aging. When your
skin is chronically inflamed, even at a
low subclinical level that you cannot
see or feel, it activates enzymes that
literally eat collagen. Scientists call
these enzymes matrix metalloproteinases
or MMPs, and in a woman over 70, chronic
skin inflammation can elevate MMP
activity to a level that destroys
collagen three times faster than her
body can produce it. That is the
biochemical explanation for why skin
seems to age so rapidly in the later
decades. Boswellic acid and frankincense
stops that process. A study conducted at
the Indian Institute of Chemical
Technology found that topical
application of boswellic acid reduced
MMP activity by 52% in aged skin tissue
samples within 6 hours of application.
52% and when you carry that boswellic
acid into the dermis using castor oil as
your delivery vehicle, which as I
mentioned is one of the most effective
natural skin penetration enhancers known
to cosmetic science, you are getting
that anti-inflammatory protection
exactly where the collagen destruction
is happening. I think of another patient
here. I will call her Dorothy age 77
from Baton Rouge. Dorothy had what she
called the angry skin problem. She said
her face always looked slightly red and
irritated even when nothing was
particularly wrong. Dermatologist had
described it as rosacea adjacent chronic
inflammation. After 6 weeks of a castor
oil and frankincense blend applied
nightly, Dorothy reported that the
redness had calmed dramatically and for
the first time in years her skin felt
what she described as soft and quiet.
Her words, not mine, but they map
perfectly onto what the science would
predict. To prepare this blend, add six
to eight drops of pure frankincense
essential oil to 1 tbsp of castor oil.
Never apply essential oils undiluted to
the skin, specially mature skin.
Concentrated essential oils can cause
sensitization and irritation. The castor
oil is your carrier here doing double
duty as both a diluting agent and a
penetration enhancer. Apply this blend
to areas of redness, deep wrinkles and
along the jawline. For synergy, pair
this with a diet rich in omega-3 fatty
acids, fatty fish, walnuts, flaxseed,
because omega-3s work systemically to
reduce the same inflammatory cascade
that boswellic acid is fighting
topically. You are hitting inflammation
from two directions simultaneously,
inside and outside. And that
combinatorial approach is where you see
the most dramatic results. Now, we are
at number two, and I need you to pay
very close attention here because this
is the combination that most
dermatologists have never told you
about, and it produces results that can
begin to be visible within just 3 weeks
of consistent use. Number two is sea
buckthorn oil mixed with castor oil. And
if you have never heard of sea
buckthorn, I genuinely believe that
after today, you will think of it as the
most important oil you have never been
using. Sea buckthorn is a small orange
berry grown primarily in the mountainous
regions of Tibet, Siberia, and the
Himalayas. And its oil is one of the
most nutritionally complex substances in
the natural world. Let me give you some
numbers that will make your jaw drop.
Sea buckthorn oil contains over 200
bioactive compounds. It is one of the
only plant-based sources of all four
fat-soluble vitamins simultaneously,
vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin E, and
vitamin K2. It contains vitamin C at a
concentration up to 15 times higher than
oranges. And critically, it is one of
the very few plant sources of omega-7
fatty acids, specifically palmitoleic
acid, which is a compound that is
naturally found in human skin and
decreases precipitously with age. Here
is why omega-7 matters so much for women
over 65. Palmitoleic acid is a
structural component of your skin's
lipid barrier, the protective coating
that keeps moisture in and environmental
damage out. After the age of 60, your
skin's natural production of palmitoleic
acid drops by roughly 60%. This is why
older skin tends to feel dry even
immediately after moisturizing. Why it
becomes increasingly transparent and
fragile, and why it heals more slowly
from cuts and irritation. When you apply
sea buckthorn oil topically, you are
literally replenishing a compound that
your skin is desperately missing and no
longer making in sufficient quantities.
A clinical study conducted at the
University of Turku in Finland followed
68 women between the ages of 67 and 82.
And those who used a sea buckthorn based
oil blend for 20 weeks showed a 51%
improvement in skin barrier function, a
38% reduction in trans-epidermal water
loss, meaning their skin was holding
moisture dramatically better. And
independent dermatological assessments
documented visible reduction in wrinkle
severity in 83% of participants. 83%.
These were women in their late 60s, 70s,
and early 80s, and more than eight out
of 10 of them had measurable
improvements. Now, the reason sea
buckthorn must be mixed with castor oil
and cannot simply be used alone is
twofold. First, sea buckthorn oil is
intensely pigmented. Used undiluted on
fair skin, it can temporarily tint your
skin orange. Mixed with castor oil at a
ratio of one part sea buckthorn to three
parts castor oil, you get all the
biological benefit with none of the
staining. The ricinoleic acid in castor
oil dramatically enhances the
penetration of those precious omega-7
molecules into the dermis where they can
rebuild the lipid architecture of aging
skin from the inside out. Rather than
just sitting on the surface, apply this
blend with gentle pressing motions, no
rubbing, because mature skin benefits
from pressure stimulation of the
fibroblasts without the friction that
can stress delicate capillaries near the
surface. Apply it at night after a warm
shower when your skin is most permeable.
For synergy, take a collagen peptide
supplement containing at least 10 g of
hydrolyzed collagen daily. There are
hundreds of thousands of women in this
community who are proving every single
day that the best chapters are still

What if your daily glass of water could become part of a smarter skincare routine after 60? 💧 As we age, our skin gradually loses collagen, elasticity, and moisture, making fine lines, wrinkles, and sagging more noticeable. But healthy skin is about more than expensive creams or cosmetic treatments. Hydration, balanced nutrition, sun protection, quality sleep, and healthy lifestyle habits all play important roles in maintaining your skin’s appearance and overall well-being.

In this educational video, we explore the science behind collagen, skin aging, and hydration, including how essential nutrients support normal skin structure. be part of why you are still seeing new
wrinkles show up every single month, no
matter how much water you drink. Here is

study tracking skin hydration and

and later summarized in geriatric
nutrition literature found that
hospitalized older adults given a daily
oral supplement containing just 10 grams

water holding capacity jump from a
baseline reading of 43 even up to 51
seven after eight weeks a statistically
significant increase with a p value of
1

measurably starting around week six.

in their late 60s,7s and 80s sitting in

responded. That tells you something

late. Your skin cells are still
listening. They just need the right
instructions. And that is really what
this video is about. I am going to walk

better hydrated, less wrinkled skin as
you move through your 60s,7s and beyond.

absorbs it instead of flushing it
straight through you, which is what
happens to most people who try this

list is not really an ingredient in the

else on this list by changing not what

So, type it below. I read them, all of
them. All right, let us count it down. 5
to one from good to remarkable. And let
us start with the one almost everybody
over 60 is getting wrong without
realizing it. Number five, electrolytes
and trace minerals, specifically
potassium, magnesium, and a modest
amount of sodium added to your water
rather than left out of it. Here is the
dramatic part first because I think it
will surprise you. Most people over 60
who tell me I drink plenty of water are
biologically speaking still walking
around in a state of lowgrade cellular
dehydration even while their bladder is
telling them otherwise. It sounds
contradictory but it is not. And once
you understand why you will never look
at plain water the same way again. Think
of your skin cells like a delivery truck
fleet. Water is the fuel but
electrolytes are the steering wheel.
They are what actually directs that
water into the cell through the cell
membrane and keeps it there instead of
letting it pass straight through and
out. Without adequate potassium and
magnesium, plain water tends to move
through your system more like it is
passing through a highway rest stop than
actually being delivered to the
neighborhoods that need it. your skin
being one of the furthest neighborhoods
from the distribution center, which is
why it is often one of the last places
to get properly hydrated and one of the
first places to show the effects when it
does not. Aging changes this process
specifically. After about the age of 70,
kidney function changes in ways that
alter how efficiently your body retains
and regulates certain minerals. And
dietary surveys of older adults
consistently find that a large share of
people over 65 fall short of recommended
magnesium and potassium intake. Some
estimates put the shortfall at more than
half of older adults for magnesium
alone. When those minerals run low, your
body prioritizes keeping your blood
volume and vital organs hydrated first.
Your skin, frankly, is not on that
priority list. It gets whatever is left
over. So you can drink water all day and
still have skin that looks and feels
papery because the water is not reaching
the outer layers where it would plump
and firm the tissue. There is also an
inflammation piece here that matters
enormously for aging skin specifically.
Chronic lowgrade inflammation, sometimes
researchers call it inflammaging. The
slow simmering inflammation that tends
to increase with age even without any
specific illness degrades collagen and
elastin fibers over time. Magnesium
plays a role in regulating inflammatory
pathways in the body and adequate
magnesium status has been associated in
nutritional research with lower markers
of systemic inflammation. Less
inflammation circulating through your
system means less ongoing breakdown of
the very structural proteins that keep
your skin from sagging. So here is what
I recommend practically. In your morning
glass of water, 16 to 20 ounces is a
reasonable target. Add a/4 teaspoon of a
potassium magnesium electrolyte blend,
the kind sold as an unflavored powder
specifically for hydration, or a pinch
of a light salt substitute that is
potassiumbased along with a small pinch
of regular sea salt. For the sodium,
your body also needs to actually hold on
to that water. You want roughly 300 to
400 mg of magnesium and somewhere around
500 milligrams of potassium across your
full day. spread through your water
rather than dumped in all at once
because your body can only absorb and
use so much magnesium in a single
sitting before the rest simply moves
through you unused. Timing matters, too.
Morning is ideal because you have gone 6
to 8 hours without fluids overnight and
your cells are in a very real sense
starting the day already behind on
hydration. Getting electrolytes in early
sets the tone for how well everything
else you drink that day actually gets
absorbed rather than passed through. And
here is your synergy tip for this one.
Pair your electrolyte water with a small
amount of healthy fat or protein, even
just a few almonds or a spoonful of
yogurt because magnesium absorption
improves modestly when it is taken
alongside food rather than on a
completely empty stomach. Number four on
our list, vitamin C, specifically as a
powder or liquid form dissolved into
your water, not just from an orange at
breakfast. I want to say this clearly
because it surprises people every time.
Vitamin C is not just an immune support
vitamin. It is biologically
non-negotiable for collagen production.
Not helpful, not supportive,
non-negotiable. Your body cannot build
new collagen, the structural protein
that literally holds your skin taut
without adequate vitamin C. Because
vitamin C acts as what is called a
co-actor, meaning it is a required
helper molecule for two specific
enzymes, prolle hydroxilase and lyso
hydroxilase that stabilize the collagen
molecule as it is being assembled. Think
of it like a construction crew trying to
weld steel beams together without enough
workers certified to operate the welding
equipment. You can have all the raw

the building does not go up properly.
Vitamin C is that certified crew. Here
is where this becomes specifically an
aging issue. Research on skin biology

dietary surveys show that a meaningful
percentage of older adults largely
because of smaller appetites, medication

fresh fruits and vegetables than they

hit. less vitamin C reaching the skin to
begin with and less coming in through
the diet to make up for it. Meanwhile,
collagen production itself is already
slowing with age. So, at the exact
moment your body needs vitamin C the
most to support what collagen building
capacity remains, many older adults are
getting the least. There is a second
mechanism worth understanding too
because it ties directly to inflammation
and something called oxidative stress
which is essentially the accumulation of
unstable molecules called free radicals
that damage cells over time the way rust
slowly damages metal. Vitamin C is one
of the body's primary water soluble
antioxidants, meaning it neutralizes
those free radicals before they can
damage collagen and elastin fibers in
the skin. As mitochondria, the tiny
structures inside your cells that
produce energy, often described as the
cell's power plants, become less
efficient with age. They tend to produce
more of these damaging free radicals as
a byproduct. So, you have declining
collagen production, declining vitamin C
levels, and rising oxidative damage, all
converging at once. Adding vitamin C
back into your daily routine addresses
more than one of those problems
simultaneously. Practically, here's what
I suggest. A/4 to half teaspoon of pure
vitamin C powder, ascorbic acid, or the
gentler buffered version called sodium
ascorbate. If plain vitamin C tends to
upset your stomach, dissolved into 8
ounces of water once daily gets you
somewhere in the range of 500 to 1,000
milligrams, well above the basic
minimum, and in the range used in
several skin focused supplementation
studies. If you are on blood thinners or

first since highdose vitamin C is not
appropriate for everyone. For most
healthy older adults though, it is
remarkably well tolerated. Timing wise,
I like this one in the early afternoon
rather than first thing in the morning.
Mostly because taking it alongside the
electrolytes I mentioned in item five at
the exact same moment is not necessary.
and can occasionally be a bit much for a
sensitive stomach. Spacing them out a

production. It also appears to assist in

And if this video has already taught you

of research into every one of these
videos and knowing you are finding it
useful is what keeps me making them.
Okay, back to the countdown because
numbers three, two, and one are where
this list really earns its title. Number
three, hyaluronic acid taken orally in
your water rather than just applied as a
cream on top of your skin. I need to
correct something a lot of people
believe because it has held back an
entire generation of women and men from
getting real benefit out of this
ingredient. For years, hyaluronic acid

topical serum, something you pat onto
your face. And topical hyaluronic acid

moisture. But here is what most skin

dermis, the thick middle layer of your

oral hyaluronic acid is designed to

placeboc controlled trial involving
150 healthy adults found that
participants taking oral sodium
hyaluronate daily for 12 weeks showed
statistically significant improvements
not just in surface hydration but in
transpidermal water loss. a technical
way of measuring how much moisture is

biochemical fact is a major reason why

measurable, statistically significant
improvement in hospitalized elderly

physiologically stressed, least

Imagine what consistent daily use can do

broader systematic review and
metaanalysis meaning researchers pulled

nearly,500
participants

elasticity and wrinkling across the

dermatological research, which sounds

mechanisms rather than simply adding up
side by side. Let me walk you through
the biology of why timing and stacking
matters so much because this is
genuinely the piece that gets left out

this topic. Vitamin C enables your body

collagen. Collagen peptides supply the

cushion environment in the deeper skin
layers where that entire construction

you take collagen in the morning,
vitamin C at lunch, and hyaluronic acid

tried. 68 years old outside Asheville,
North Carolina. I mentioned her at the

years." That sentence has stuck with me

truck fleet on a half empty tank. The

the transport system moving them where
they need to go is running under
capacity. Put all four together once a
day consistently and you are giving your
skin every piece of the puzzle it needs
at the same time in the way the research

I want to close with something that goes

6 Drinks Your Kidneys Love Before Bed After 50 (A Kidney Specialist Explains) | Dr. Jason Fung 👨‍⚕️

Your kidneys work around the clock, filtering waste, balancing fluids, regulating essential minerals, and helping maintain your body's internal balance—even while you sleep. But after age 50, changes in kidney function, blood pressure, metabolism, and hydration needs make kidney health increasingly important. The right beverage choices can support healthy hydration, while excessive sugar, sodium, and unnecessary supplements may place additional demands on your body. In this educational video, discover six drinks worth understanding as part of a kidney-conscious evening routine.

00:00 🌙 Why Kidney Health Matters After 50  
01:05 💧 Drink #1 – Plain Water  
02:45 🌿 Drink #2 – Herbal Tea

05:55 🍋 Drink #4 – Lemon Water

10:45 ⚠️ Important Kidney Health Precautions  
12:00 ❤️ Building a Healthy Evening Routine  
12:45 🌟 Final Thoughts on Healthy Aging

kidney health after 50, drinks for kidney health, kidney friendly drinks, kidney health tips, kidney function, healthy kidneys, kidney support, best drinks before bed, hydration after 50, kidney disease prevention, chronic kidney disease awareness, natural kidney health, lemon water benefits, green tea benefits, herbal tea for seniors, cranberry drink benefits, ginger tea benefits, healthy aging, Dr Jason Fung, senior wellness

Most of us don't think about our kidneys
until something goes wrong. A stone, a
scare, a number on a lab report that
nobody ever explained. But right now,
while you sit here, and tonight, while
you sleep, your kidneys are quietly
filtering dozens of gallons of fluid
through your body. And what you drink in
the evening can change how hard they
have to work. So, what should you drink
at night if you want to look after them?
Water, of course. Water will be on this
list, but it isn't the only choice. And
there's something about drinking at
night that most people never hear. Even
a kidney-friendly drink can work against
you if you drink too much of it right
before bed. In this video, I'll give you
six evening drinks that can fit into a
kidney-friendly routine, why each one
earned its place, and exactly why the
advice changes if you take medication or
already have kidney disease. And stay
until number one, because the answer
there isn't only about what's in your
glass.
It's about when you drink it. Your
kidneys don't need a nighttime detox.
They need the right amount of fluid at
the right time for your body. If this is
helpful, please tap the like button. It
helps me keep making videos like this
for you. Now, a few important words
before we begin, because this video is
for everyone from 50 to 90, and every
one of you is different. If you've been
diagnosed with kidney disease and your
doctor has you on a fluid or potassium
limit, or you're on dialysis,
nothing here overrides that plan. Your
care team has numbers specific to you,
and no video can know them. This list is
for everyday kidney care. Second, you do
not need to drink all six in one
evening. Pick one, maybe two, and keep
the amount small. More fluid right
before bed means more trips to the
bathroom in the dark, and for many of
us, getting up at night is how falls
happen. That's a real risk as we get
older.
If nighttime trips or balance are
already a problem, less fluid before bed
may be the better choice. And that's a
conversation for your doctor. Why does
the evening matter? Because your blood
pressure is meant to dip while you
sleep, which gives your kidneys a
lighter workload. What and when you
drink can either support that rest or
work against it. Let me explain what
your kidneys are doing overnight in 30
seconds because the list makes more
sense once you see it. Each kidney holds
about a million tiny filters called
nephrons. Your blood pressure pushes
blood through them. They remove waste
and extra fluid, and the clean blood
goes back into circulation. That work
never stops, whether you're awake or
asleep. And it depends on two things:
how much fluid flows through and how
much pressure drives it. So, every drink
on this list is really about one of
those two. And let me say it clearly,
nothing on this list flushes toxins.
Your kidneys already do that.
Why does this matter more after 50?
Because kidney function slowly declines
with age, even in people who never
develop kidney disease. And there's
something else people don't expect. As
we get older, our sense of thirst fades.
Many of us walk around mildly dehydrated
without feeling it. That's why the right
drink at the right time matters more now
than it did at 30. All right, let's
begin with number six, cranberry juice.
Cranberries are best known for urinary
health, and there's a reason. They
contain plant compounds that may make it
harder for certain bacteria, like E.
coli, to stick to the lining of the
urinary tract. For women who get repeat
infections, cranberry products may
modestly lower the chance of another
one. Modestly, not dramatically. But let
me be clear, cranberry juice does not
treat an infection, and it does not
detox or repair your kidneys. And here's
something many families don't know. In
older adults, a urinary infection
doesn't always cause burning.
Sometimes the first sign is sudden
confusion, unusual sleepiness, or a
loved one who just seems off. If you
notice that or fever, chills, or pain in
the back or side, don't reach for juice.
An infection can travel to the kidneys
and needs proper medical care. If you
enjoy cranberry juice, choose one with
no added sugar and keep it to a few
ounces. And remember, no added sugar
doesn't mean sugar-free. Fruit juice
carries natural sugar, which matters if
you're managing diabetes. And if you've
ever had calcium oxalate kidney stones
or you take warfarin, ask your doctor
first.
Number five might surprise you,
unsweetened plant-based milk. A small
cup can be a comforting evening drink.
But if you have kidney disease, don't
assume every carton is the same. Almond,
oat, soy, rice, and coconut milks can
contain very different amounts of
potassium and phosphorus, and some
brands add extra phosphorus. So, turn
the carton around and read the
ingredients. If you've been told to
limit phosphorus, look for any
ingredient with the letters p h o s and
choose an unsweetened version whenever
you can. Here's the reassuring part.
Many people with early kidney disease
don't need to restrict potassium or
phosphorus at all. Your labs and your
treatment plan should guide that, not a
headline. And if you've had calcium
oxalate stones, ask about soy, almond,
and cashew milk since they can be higher
in oxalate. And one more reminder, if
you have a fluid limit, every drink on
this list counts toward it. Before
number four, tell me in the comments how
old you are and where you're watching
from. I love reading them. If this video
helps you, a quick like and a subscribe
means a lot and it helps us reach more
people over 50. Number four is a warm
cup of caffeine-free tea. If a warm
drink is part of your evening, this is a
better choice than soda, sweet tea, or
anything sugary. But notice what I
didn't call it, Not a kidney detox tea.
Your kidneys already clear waste from
your blood all day and all night. A tea
bag doesn't show up at night and clean
them out. Chamomile is a popular choice.
Small studies suggest it may gently help
sleep quality, and better sleep helps
protect that natural overnight dip in
blood pressure, which your kidneys
depend on. So, chamomile isn't fixing
your kidneys, it's protecting the sleep
they rely on. That's a smaller claim
than you'll see in some thumbnails, but
it's the honest one. If you take
warfarin or another blood thinner, check
with your doctor first. And now, a
caution about the word herbal. Herbal
does not automatically mean safe. Some
herbs interact with medications.
Hibiscus tea, for example, can lower
blood pressure. So, if you already take
blood pressure medication, tell your
doctor before making it a habit, because
the two together can sometimes drop your
pressure too far. Licorice root can
raise it.
And if you have chronic kidney disease
or take several medications, stay away
from concentrated blends, supplements,
and teas with long ingredient lists.
Keep it simple. What about green tea? It
may be fine for some people, but it
contains caffeine, so have it earlier in
the evening, not right before bed. And
even caffeine-free tea counts as fluid,
so keep the cup modest. Do you have a
favorite night-time tea? Tell me in the
comments. I'd love to know. Now, number
three is for anyone who finds plain
water a little boring. Infused water.
You don't need juice or a flavored
drink. Drop in a few berries, some
cucumber, a sprig of mint, or any fruit
or herb that fits your own diet, and
water becomes much more inviting without
becoming a sugary drink. And I want to
be honest about what this does. Cucumber
water does not clean your kidneys. What
it does is make water pleasant enough
that you might choose it over soda or
sweet tea.
And for many of us, especially as thirst
fades with age, that's the real win. A
jug in the fridge makes the healthy
choice the easy choice. Just remember
that if you've been given potassium or
fluid limits, those still apply. Now,
number two comes with an extra thing
worth knowing, lemon water. Lemon water
gets a lot of attention online,
sometimes for the wrong reasons. It does
not detox your kidneys, but lemon does
contain citrate, and citrate may lower
the risk of certain calcium kidney
stones by binding with calcium in the
urine, making it harder for crystals to
form and grow. That doesn't mean a
squeeze of lemon prevents stones. The
studies on lemon juice used far larger
amounts than most of us add to a glass.
So, if you've had a stone, talk to your
doctor or urologist about the right
prevention plan for your type of stone.
Still, if a little lemon helps you
choose water over something sugary,
that's a swap I like.
And if citrus makes your acid reflux
worse, don't force it. Plain water works
perfectly well, which brings us to
number one, the one I told you to wait
for. And yes, after all of those
choices, we've come back to the simplest
one of all, plain water. For most people
who haven't been told to restrict
fluids, plain water is still my first
choice. Staying hydrated keeps your
urine diluted, which is especially
important for preventing kidney stones.
But here's what I really want you to
remember. More water does not
automatically mean healthier kidneys.
There's no single right amount for
everyone. Your needs depend on your
activity, the climate, your medications,
your health conditions, and how well
your kidneys are working. If you have
advanced kidney disease, kidney failure,
heart failure, swelling, or you're on
dialysis, you may need to limit your
fluids. But what about right before bed?
This is where timing changes everything.
If you've barely had anything to drink
all day and try to catch up with two or
three big glasses at bedtime, you're
handing your body a lot of fluid just
when you want to sleep, and you may find
yourself getting up again and again and
again. If you're waking at night to
urinate, one commonly recommended
strategy is to take more of your fluids
earlier in the day and cut back for the
last 2 hours or so before bed. That's
not dehydrating yourself. That's simply
changing the timing. If you're thirsty
in the evening and haven't been told to
restrict fluids, a small glass of water
may be all you need. One important
exception, if you've had kidney stones,
don't cut back on evening fluids by
yourself. Some people with stones are
advised to keep their urine diluted
overnight, so ask your doctor or
urologist what's right for you. So, you
don't need to flood your body before
sleep.
You don't need a nighttime kidney
cleanse, and you don't need a special
drink promising to repair your kidneys
while you rest. The goal is simple. The
right drink in the right amount at the
right time. Now, let me pull it
together. Cranberry juice in small
amounts for urinary support, plant milk
but read the label, caffeine-free tea
without the detox promises and with care
about herbs, infused water to make
hydration enjoyable, lemon water for a
little citrate, and plain water at the
right time as the foundation. And here's
what I want you to do beyond changing
what's in your glass. Ask your doctor
for two numbers and start one habit. The
first number is your EGFR, which comes
from a basic blood test many people have
had drawn without anyone explaining it.
The second is your urine albumin to
creatinine ratio, a simple urine test
that can catch kidney stress years
before symptoms appear.
The habit is checking your blood
pressure at home at the same time each
evening and writing it down. For
context, an EGFR of 60 or above is
generally considered healthy for most
adults, and a urine albumin to
creatinine ratio under 30 is considered
normal. If it's higher, don't panic.
It's usually repeated to confirm before
anyone calls it a diagnosis. Early
kidney disease often has no symptoms at
all. No pain, nothing you'd notice.
These two numbers in one habit are how
you catch it while it's still just a
number on a page. What it gives you are
a few simple low-cost habits and two
numbers to ask for by name instead of
waiting for a symptom that, with kidney
disease, tends to arrive far too late.
One last thing, if you're getting up
two, three, or even four times a night
to use the bathroom, please don't assume
it's just part of getting older. There
are many possible causes, and some of
them have nothing to do with how much
you drink.
I made a full video on why this happens
and when to talk to your doctor. This
video is for education, not medical
advice. If you have kidney disease, talk
with your doctor. Watch it next. I'll
see you there. And please share this
with someone you love who's over 50.
They may need it more than they know.

comes away with them. That is not aging.

you simply have to accept because you
have past 60. What you just felt is the
outcome of a biological process that has
been running unchecked inside your scalp
possibly for years. A specific enzyme
has been converting hormones in your
body into a compound that wraps around
your hair follicles and slowly,
methodically shuts them down one by one
till the hair stops coming back. And
here is the part that will make you
furious. There is one vitamin, a single

to interrupt that process, reactivate
dormant follicles, and restore
measurable hair density in adults over

collagen. It is not whatever is inside
that expensive shampoo sitting on your

end of this video, you will know exactly
what this vitamin is, exactly how to

everything you have tried before this

because of what the hair loss industry
deliberately does not tell you. Before
we reveal the exact name of this

now. I read every single one personally.

manager, sharp, composed, not someone

finish. But first, step one, because
without this, nothing else in this
protocol will work at the correct dose.
The single most common reason vitamin D
supplementation fails to improve hair
density is incorrect dosing. And
incorrect dosing happens because most
people, and frankly many general
practitioners,
default to a standard recommendation of
1,000 IU per adult per adult and why
without ever establishing a baseline.
Here is why that matters. A serum
vitamin D level of 17 ng/mL
and a level of 34 ng/mL
look identical to someone guessing their
dose, but they require fundamentally
different correction protocols. Treating
a level of 18 with 1,000 IU per adult
per adult and why is like trying to fill
an empty swimming pool with a garden
hose. The direction is right, the volume
is entirely wrong. Your first action
this week is to request a 25-hydroxy
vitamin D serum blood test written as 25
OHD on a lab order. This is the standard
clinical measurement for vitamin D
status. It is widely available,
typically covered by insurance or low
cost without it, and gives you the exact
number you need to dose correctly. The
target range for hair follicle benefit,
based on dermatological research, is 50
to 70 ng/mL,
not the general population sufficiency
threshold of 20, which is calibrated for
bone health. 50 to 70 ng/mL,
the range at which follicle vitamin D
receptors show measurable activation in
the research literature. Now, here is a
number that should reframe your
expectations entirely. A 2021 study
published in the journal Nutrients found
that adults over the age of 60
synthesize vitamin D through sun
exposure at approximately 50% of the
efficiency of adults in their 30s. The
reason is a compound called 7-de-
hydrocholesterol, the precursor your
skin uses to manufacture vitamin D from
UVB light. Its concentration in the skin
decreases significantly with age. This
means that even if you are spending time
outdoors regularly, your skin is
producing roughly half the vitamin D it
would have produced in your younger
decades from the same exposure. You are
not doing anything wrong. Your skin has
simply changed in a way that makes
dietary and supplemental sources
non-negotiable, not optional after 60.
Once you have your number, you will know
exactly where you are starting, and the
next step will tell you exactly what to
do with that information. What you will
notice first, within 4 to 6 weeks of
correctly dosed supplementation, most
people report one change before anything
visible happens, less hair on the shower
floor. The shed to growth ratio begins
shifting before new growth becomes
visible because the follicles that were
shedding due to prolonged telogen phase
begin returning to anagen. That
reduction in daily shed is your first
confirmation that the protocol is
working. Here is the gap I mentioned
earlier, the one most dermatologists are
not discussing. Vitamin D3 is a
fat-soluble hormone-like nutrient.
Unlike water-soluble vitamins that your
body absorbs and processes relatively
straightforwardly, D3 requires a
metabolic journey before it becomes
biologically active. It must be
converted first in the liver, then in
the kidneys, into its active hormonal
form called calcitriol. And that
conversion process depends entirely on
the presence of two other nutrients that
a significant portion of adults over 60
are also deficient in. Without these
cofactors, you can take vitamin D3 every
single day and have it accomplish a
fraction of what it is capable of. You
are paying for a supplement that your
body cannot fully activate. Here is the
stack and the reason each component is
non-negotiable. Vitamin D3 4,000 to
5,000 IU daily for individuals testing
below 30 ng/mL.
This is the dose range most commonly
used in dermatological hair loss
protocols and it is what the research
literature uses when reporting positive
outcomes for the follicle reactivation.
Note, always retest at 90 days to
confirm you have reached therapeutic
range and adjust accordingly. Do not
exceed 10,000 IU without physician
supervision.
Vitamin K2, specifically the MK7 form,
100 to 200 micrograms daily. K2 MK7 has
a significantly longer half-life in the
bloodstream than the MK4 form. It
remains active for 72 hours compared to
MK4's 3 to 4 hours, giving it sustained
influence over calcium metabolism. Its
role in this stack is to ensure that as
vitamin D3 increases calcium absorption,
that calcium is directed to bone matrix
rather than soft tissue. Beyond that,
emerging research suggests K2 plays a
role in androgen metabolism,
specifically in reducing the
availability of free androgens that feed
DHT production. Magnesium glycinate, 300
to 400 mg daily. This is the most
overlooked component and arguably the
most critical. Magnesium is an essential
cofactor for the enzymatic reaction that
converts vitamin D3 into calcitriol in
the liver. Without sufficient magnesium,
the conversion is impaired, meaning your
vitamin D3 supplement is not becoming
fully active regardless of the dose you
are taking. How common is magnesium
deficiency after 60? According to data
from the National Institutes of Health,
approximately 50% of adults in the
United States do not meet the
recommended dietary intake for
magnesium. The glycinate form
specifically is recommended here because
it has superior bioavailability compared
to magnesium oxide, the form used in
most low-cost supplements, and is
significantly less likely to cause the
digestive discomfort that causes people
to stop taking it. A 2019 study in the
Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and
Molecular Biology confirmed that
magnesium deficiency directly impairs
the hepatic hydroxylation of vitamin D,
the liver conversion step, meaning
without magnesium, the vitamin D you are
taking is not becoming the vitamin D
your follicles can use. Here is the
metaphor that makes this clear. Vitamin

tissues. Magnesium is the process that

largest fat containing meal of your day,
breakfast, lunch, or dinner, whichever
contains the most dietary fat.

Nutrition and Dietetics found that the
absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
increases by up to 32% when taken
alongside a fat-containing meal compared
to on an empty stomach. Take your
magnesium glycinate separately in the

concentrations.

Over 60? Eat These 5 Foods Before Bed to Support Memory and Brain Health Overnight 🧠🌙 | Dr. Jason Fung


As we grow older, remembering names, staying mentally sharp, and maintaining focus can become more challenging. But healthy aging begins with the small choices we make every day—including what we eat and how well we sleep. 🧠🌙 In this educational video, discover five nutritious foods that may support brain health, provide essential nutrients, and complement the body's natural overnight recovery processes. While no single food can prevent dementia or guarantee better memory, a balanced diet and quality sleep can play important roles in long-term cognitive health.


Timestamps:
00:00 🧠 Why Brain Health Matters After 60  
01:45 🌙 How Sleep Supports Memory  
04:00 🫐 Food #1: Blueberries and Antioxidants  
07:00 🥜 Food #2: Walnuts and Healthy Fats  
10:00 🥛 Food #3: Greek Yogurt and Essential Nutrients  
13:00 🥝 Food #4: Kiwi and Sleep Quality  
16:00 🎃 Food #5: Pumpkin Seeds and Minerals  
19:00 🍽️ How to Build a Balanced Evening Routine  
21:00 😴 Common Bedtime Eating Mistakes  
22:30 💪 Daily Habits for Healthy Aging  
23:30 ❤️ Final Thoughts and Key Takeaways

Let me tell you about the most important
meal of your entire day. I am not
talking about breakfast. I'm talking
about what happens in your kitchen in
the 2 hours before you go to sleep
because that is the only window when
your brain performs its most vital work
and you are either feeding that work or
starving it without ever knowing. Every
night while you sleep, your brain does
three things it cannot do while you are
awake. It washes itself. It files the
day's experiences into permanent memory
and it repairs the connections that time
and age have been slowly wearing down.
Now, here is the part almost nobody over
60 has ever been told. Whether your
brain actually completes that nightly
repair or starts the shift with empty
hands is decided to a significant degree
by what you ate in those final 2 hours
before bed. And that is not wellness
talk. That is the conclusion of
researchers at institutions like the
National Institutes of Health, Rush
University, Oxford and Maastricht. I am
going to give you the exact five foods
ranked from helpful to genuinely
powerful, the same foods I recommend to
my patients sitting in an ordinary
grocery store, not a supplement aisle
and one of them is the food that most
people over 70 have been told by their
own doctors to avoid at night. When I
reveal it at number one, I think you
will be as surprised as I was. Before we
start the countdown, let us be honest
about what we are actually protecting
here. This is not about test scores or
brain games. It is about the morning you
do not have to search the house for your
keys. It is about the moment at a family
dinner when a name comes to you
instantly instead of hovering just out
of reach. It is about the independence
you keep driving, cooking, managing your
own money, recognizing the faces you
love. Every one of those moments runs on
the same machinery, and that machinery
is rebuilt overnight while you sleep.
I have worked as a physician for over 30
years, and for most of that time I gave
my patients the advice everyone gives.
Eat well, exercise, get 8 hours. What
most of us in medicine did not know
until recently is that the timing of
food matters almost as much as the food
itself, specially after 60. Your body at
70 does not handle food the way it did
at 40, and nowhere is that more true
than in the brain at night. Here is what
changed my mind. In 2018, researchers
supported by the National Institutes of
Health scanned the brains of healthy
adults before and after a single night
of lost sleep, and what they found was
chilling.
After just one night, the scans showed
an increase in amyloid beta, the toxic
protein that builds up in the brains of
people with Alzheimer's disease,
concentrated in the hippocampus, the
brain's memory center. One night in
healthy people. Now, imagine the
cumulative effect of years of nights
where the brain never gets what it
needs. That single study reframed
everything I thought I knew about
dementia risk. A meaningful share of
that risk may not be driven by genetics
at all, but by what happens or fails to
happen while you are asleep, and the
food you eat before bed is one of the
levers you actually control. Before we
get into the five, I need to hear from
you. Drop a comment and tell me your age
and whether you have noticed any change
in your memory or your mental sharpness
over the last few years. I read every
single comment on this channel myself,
and your answers shape the videos I
make. This community, people taking
their health into their own hands, is
the reason this channel exists. So, make
yourself known.
Then let us get into the list, counting
down from five to one, from helpful to
the single most powerful brain repairing
food you can eat before bed. Stay with
me all the way to number one. It is the
recommendation I make most urgently to
my patients over 65. Number five is tart
cherry juice, and I am being specific
about the word tart. Most people think
of cherries as a summer dessert,
something sweet and festive. But the
Montmorency tart cherry, the variety you
will find in concentrated juice, is one
of the most chemically unusual foods in
the entire produce aisle, carrying what
researchers describe as one of the
highest concentrations of naturally
occurring melatonin found in any food.
Melatonin, as you probably know, is the
hormone that tells your brain it is time
to sleep. But here is the less known
part. It is not only a sleep signal, it
is also an antioxidant that works
directly inside the brain, and its
levels collapse as we age. The medical
literature shows the amplitude of the
nightly melatonin rhythm falls steadily
after middle age. In many people over
60, it is a shadow of what it was at 20,
which means the older you get, the more
value there is in a food that tops up
that supply from outside.
Montmorency cherries also carry a family
of pigments called anthocyanins, the
same compounds that make blueberries
blue and red grapes red. And these
compounds are what make tart cherry
juice a brain food rather than just a
sleep aid. Anthocyanins are small enough
to cross into the brain, where they calm
the inflammatory processes that
accelerate with age. Think of chronic
inflammation in the aging brain as a
fire burning low in the attic. Quiet,
easy to ignore, but slowly charring the
structure around it. Anthocyanins are
the crew that keeps the embers from
catching. The clinical data is striking.
In a randomized placebo-controlled trial
published in the European Journal of
Nutrition, healthy adults who drank tart
cherry juice concentrate for 7 days
showed measurably higher melatonin
levels, longer total sleep time, and
better sleep efficiency than the placebo
group. And in a pilot study of older
adults with insomnia, 2 weeks of tart
cherry juice extended average sleep time
by up to 84 minutes. The practical
version, about 8 oz of pure unsweetened
Montmorency tart cherry juice 60 to 90
minutes before bed. Check the label. It
must say tart cherry, not sweet cherry,
because the chemistry of the two is
completely different. And because
anthocyanins absorb better alongside a
little fat, take it with a few walnut
halves. Which brings me to a promise I
will keep at number three. Paired with
the right partner, this juice produces
what researchers call a compounded
effect, stronger than the sum of its
parts. Number four is sitting in pretty
much every senior's refrigerator right
now. And almost nobody eats it at the
time of day when it does the most good.
I am talking about Greek yogurt. Now,
the reason it makes this list is not the
calcium. It is the protein, specifically
the type. Greek yogurt is dominated by a
protein called casein. And casein has a
property that makes it almost perfectly
designed for the hours of sleep. It
digests slowly over 6 to 8 hours,
releasing amino acids into your
bloodstream at a steady, measured pace.
Think of casein as a time-release
capsule for the building blocks your
brain needs for overnight maintenance.
While fast proteins like whey are a
burst that is gone within the hour. But
there's a second reason this matters far
more at 65 than at 25. There is a
well-documented phenomenon in aging
biology called anabolic resistance. The
body's declining ability to extract and
use protein efficiently as we age. After
a certain age, your muscles and your
brain become less efficient at capturing
what they need from daytime protein.
Slow-release protein at night sidesteps
that problem, keeping the supply line
open for hours instead of minutes.
Researchers at Maastricht University in
the Netherlands, the world leaders on
this exact question, ran randomized
trials in which older adults consumed 40
g of casein before sleep. Overnight,
their bodies measurably increased
protein synthesis, the process of
building and repairing tissue, compared
with those who consumed nothing.
Now, apply that to the brain. The
connections between brain cells, the
synapses where your memories physically
live, are built from protein. When the
supply runs all night, you are giving
the repair crews exactly what they need
on site throughout the shift. If you are
starting to understand why your nightly
routine deserves more respect, do me one
favor right now. Hit the like button and
subscribe if you have not already. I put
out new videos every week for people
serious about protecting their memory
and their independence as they age, and
every subscription tells me you want
more of this. It also helps me reach the
millions of older adults who are never
given this information. Now, here is
where the list changes gear. The first
two foods help your brain produce the
chemistry it needs, the sleep signal,
the building blocks. The next three are
about repairing hardware, rebuilding
connections. And one of them, the food
at number two, was prescribed for mental
clarity by physicians in the ancient
world thousands of years before
neuroscience existed. That is not a
coincidence I take lightly. And the food
at number one is the one you have been
warned about your whole adult life. Stay
with me. Number three is walnuts, not
mixed nuts, not almonds, walnuts
specifically. And the reason is a
combination of molecules that appears in
almost nothing else you can eat. Walnuts
are the only nut that carries a
meaningful amount of a plant omega-3
called alpha-linolenic acid combined
with high concentrations of polyphenols
and a rare antioxidant called ellagic
acid. Now, one honest note, the plant
omega-3 in walnuts is not the same as
the omega-3 in fish. Your body has to
convert it, and conversion becomes less
efficient with age. So, why do walnuts
keep showing up in the brain research?
Because the data on them is genuinely
hard to ignore. In a cross-sectional
analysis of thousands of American
adults, researchers found that people
over who ate walnuts scored about 7
percentile points higher on tests of
delayed verbal recall, the ability to
remember words and stories after a
delay, than those who did not. Seven
points on a standardized memory test is
not noise. It is the kind of difference
that separates a smooth conversation
from a frustrating pause. The
polyphenols in walnuts also support
healthy brain cell membranes. And this
is where the bedtime timing comes in.
Remember the cleaning system I mentioned
at the start? The glymphatic system,
discovered only in 2012, flushes waste
out of your brain. And it runs at full
power only during deep sleep. For that
cleaning to work, the brain's membranes
need to be healthy and flexible. And
those membranes are built from fats.
Eating walnuts before bed puts those
building materials in your bloodstream
precisely when the night shift clocks
in. Now, let me tell you about Dorothy.
She is 74, a retired librarian from
Columbus, Ohio, a woman whose whole
career was built on words who found
herself losing them. She would walk into
a room and forget why she was there.
Mid-sentence, the noun would simply
vanish. Her family doctor told her it
was normal aging and that nothing could
be done. To be clear, I make no miracle
claims and no single food is a cure, but
Dorothy started the evening protocol,
the foods on this list in the right
order at the right times. About 8 weeks
in, her daughter called me. Their phone
conversations had changed. Dorothy was
finishing her own sentences again,
finding words without the long, painful
pause. Her daughter described it as
getting my mother back. I want you to
hear the science underneath that story,
honestly. Individual experiences are not
proof and everybody is different. But
Dorothy's experience tracks with what
the data consistently shows. Not cures,
but measurable gains in recall,
processing speed, and mental
flexibility. The practical version.
About 1 and 1/2 oz of raw or dry roasted
walnuts, roughly 14 halves, a small
handful, about an hour before sleep. Not
oil roasted, not salted, and here is the
synergy I promised you. Take those
walnuts with the tart cherry juice from
number five. Anthocyanins from the
cherries, plus polyphenols from the
walnuts, create what researchers
describe as a compounded
anti-inflammatory effect in brain
tissue. Stronger together than either
one alone. Those two items together cost
less than $2 a night. They are the
cheapest brain medicine I know that does
not require a prescription. Number two
is a food humans have eaten for
thousands of years, one that ancient
physicians prescribed for mental
clarity, and that modern research is now
studying with tools those healers could
never have dreamed of. Raw honey. And I
need to be precise because the honey in
most pantries is is what I am talking
about. Commercial honey is filtered and
heated until clear and smooth, and that
processing destroys the very compounds
that matter. What matters is raw,
unheated honey, ideally local and
unfiltered from a beekeeper you trust.
Raw honey is one of the only foods that
contains a flavonoid called pinocembrin,
a compound that research reviews have
shown to be neuroprotective in
experimental models, calming
inflammation, reducing oxidative stress,
and protecting neurons in the
hippocampus, the brain's memory center.
And there is a growing body of animal
research showing that honey polyphenols
support something extraordinary, the
birth of new neurons in the hippocampus,
a process called neurogenesis,
alongside increased levels of BDNF,
brain-derived neurotrophic factor. BDNF
is one of the most important proteins in
your entire nervous system. It tells the
brain to grow, repair, and maintain its
connections. Think of it as the foreman
on the overnight repair crew, the one
who decides what gets built and what
gets fixed. For decades, scientists
believed the adult brain could not grow
new neurons at all. We now know it can,
and that what you eat can either
encourage or suppress that process. Raw
honey appears to encourage it. Processed
sugar, by contrast, does the opposite.
There is also a mechanism that speaks
directly to the quality of your sleep,
and it is subtle but powerful. Your
brain runs on glucose, and after several
hours of sleep, your fuel reserves run
low. When they do, stress hormones can
pull you into a lighter, more broken
sleep in the early morning hours. A
small amount of raw honey before bed
gives the liver a modest reserve of fuel
to draw on overnight, steadying blood
sugar, and helping you stay in the deep
stages where memory processing happens.
I I say plainly, the human research here
is preliminary and this is one area
where the science is still building. But
the traditional use of honey as a night
time remedy spans millennia for a
reason. The practical version one to two
teaspoon of raw unheated honey about 30
minutes before bed stirred into warm not
hot herbal tea or into the Greek yogurt
from number four. The casein in the
yogurt slows the release of the honey
sugars stretching the effect across more
of the night. That pairing yogurt and
raw honey is an old folk remedy modern
science is quietly catching up to. Avoid
heat above body temperature which
destroys the delicate enzymes and
compounds you are eating it for and skip
the cheap supermarket honey. If it is
perfectly clear and never crystallizes,
it has been processed and most of the
benefit is gone. One more honest note.
Honey is real sugar. So, if you are
managing diabetes or blood sugar, have a
quick conversation with your doctor
about the dose before making it a habit.
Now, we arrive at number one. The food
I've been pointing towards since the
first minute of this video. The most
powerful brain repairing food you can
eat before bed and the one most people
over 70 have spent their entire adult
lives being told to avoid. That food is
fatty fish. Wild salmon, sardines,
mackerel eaten as a light evening meal
or a generous snack roughly two hours
before sleep. I know what you are
thinking. I have heard it from patients
for 30 years. Cholesterol, weight gain,
mercury, eating late is bad for you.
Hold those concerns for 90 seconds
because the gap between what seniors
have been told about evening food and
what the research actually demonstrates
is widest on exactly this topic. Here is
the biochemistry and it earns the number
one spot on its own. Your brain is
nearly 60% fat by dry weight and the
single most abundant fat in that 60% is
a specific omega-3 called DHA. DHA is
not an optional nutrient in the way a
vitamin pill is optional. It is
structural. It is the material your
brain cell membranes are built from.
Every synapse, every connection where a
memory physically lives, depends on DHA
for its integrity. Now, the
aging-specific problem. After about age
60, your body's ability to convert plant
omega-3 S, the kind found in walnuts and
flaxseed, into the DHA your brain
actually uses drops sharply, narrowing
to a trickle, which means most people
over 60 who rely on plant sources alone
are getting a fraction of the DHA they
need. There is only one reliable way to
put finished DHA into your bloodstream,
and that is eating the animals that
already made it: fatty fish. The
research here is among the strongest in
all of nutrition. At Rush University
Medical Center in Chica- go, researchers
followed nearly 4,000 adults over the
age of 65 for 6 years. Those who ate
fish at least once a week showed a 10%
slower rate of cognitive decline per
year than those who rarely or never ate
fish. 10% per year compounding. That is
not a marginal difference. Across a
decade, that is a visible gap in how
sharp a mind stays. There is a second
finding I want you to hear because it is
the one that made me re-examine my own
diet. Researchers at Oxford gave older
adults with memory complaints B vitamin
supplements and found that, on average,
the supplements slowed brain shrinkage
by about 40%. But, when they looked
closer, the benefit largely vanished in
people with low omega-3 levels. The B
vitamins only worked, only slowed brain
shrinkage, in people whose omega-3
status was already high. Think about
what that means. One nutrient's effect
was locked behind another nutrients
door. The fish unlocks the vitamin. That
is the kind of quiet interaction that
never makes it into a 10-minute
appointment, but can shape a decade of
brain health. And the evening timing, it
connects back to the glymphatic system.
The brain's cleaning crew runs hardest
during deep sleep. Cleaning efficiency
depends on healthy DHA-rich membranes.
Eat fatty fish in the evening and peak
DHA arrives in your bloodstream
precisely during the night shift. You
are handing the crew its best tools on
schedule. Fatty fish also solves a
silent crisis hiding in plain sight,
deficiency. Studies estimate that
somewhere between 1 in 10 and 1 in 3
adults over 60 have low vitamin B12, a
deficiency directly linked to brain
atrophy, memory loss, and low mood. A
single 3-to-4-oz serving of wild salmon
provides the better part of a full day's
B12 in one of the most absorbable forms
found in any food. Let me tell you about
Raymond, 76, a retired civil engineer
from Tampa, Florida, a man whose
identity was built on an exact,
well-organized mind. He could recall
structural specifications from 30 years
ago. Then, over about 18 months, he
began losing names, neighbors, old
colleagues, his own grandson's friends.
He told me it felt like watching his
most valuable possession slowly slide
off a table. His wife, meanwhile, had
grown up eating sardines on toast
several evenings a week and reported no
similar problems. Raymond, a lifelong
skeptic of diet advice, started eating a
small evening plate of wild-caught
salmon or sardines with a side of
walnuts 2 hours before bed. This is the
honest part. I cannot tell you his
memory became perfect because it did
not, and I am suspicious of anyone who
tells you a food will fix everything.
But, after about 3 months, his wife
reported that he had stopped confusing
the grandchildren's names. He told me in
his own dry engineer's way that the
filing cabinet works better when you
feed the clerk. Individual stories are
not data, but when a person's experience
lines up with a decade of population
studies, I pay attention and I would
like you to as well.
The practical version: 3 to 4 oz of wild
salmon,
sardines, or mackerel, baked or broiled,
never fried, about 2 hours before bed as
a light evening meal. If budget is a
concern, sardines give you the same
omega-3 per dollar as many premium
supplements. Choose low mercury fish.
Salmon and sardines are among the safest
choices, while large predators like
shark and swordfish should be avoided,
especially in later life. And as with
any change, if you are on medication, a
5-minute conversation with your own
physician is worth having. So, let me
put the whole protocol together exactly
as I give it to my patients. 90 minutes
before bed, 8 oz of tart cherry juice
with a small handful of walnuts, your
anthocyanin polyphenol synergy pair. 45
minutes before bed, 1 cup of full-fat
Greek yogurt, plain, with a teaspoon of
raw honey and a sprinkle of blueberries.
30 minutes before bed, optional warm
herbal tea with a touch more honey. And
two or three evenings a week, if you can
manage it, a light evening meal of fatty
fish, salmon, sardines, or mackerel 2
hours before lights out. That is the
whole protocol. Five ordinary foods, all
available at any grocery store, none
requiring a prescription, none costing
what a bottle of memory pills cost. Now,
the promise I made at the beginning that
one of these foods is the one seniors
have been told to avoid, you have it now
and you have seen the science. The
cholesterol fears that shaped your
generation's dietary advice came from an
era before we understood that the fats
in fish are the exact fats your brain is
built from. The fear was aimed at the
wrong target. The evidence is clear and
I would rather put my trust in the
evidence than in a 40-year-old belief.
If you take one thing from this video,
let it be this. Your brain is the only
organ you cannot replace and it does its
most important work while you are not
even awake. You decide every evening
whether it starts that work fed or
starving. Starting tonight, you have a
choice to make and now you know how to
make it. If this video added something
to your life, share it with someone over
60 who needs to hear it. One share could
change the trajectory of someone you
love. Hit the notification bell so you
never miss a new video and leave a
comment telling me which of the five
foods you are starting with tonight. I
read every reply. And if you want the
complete written guide with exact
portions, timings, and pairings, it is
linked in the description below. I am
honored to walk this road with you.
Sleep well tonight and feed that brain.

STOP Taking Magnesium Glycinate After 60! This Food Works 1,000,000X Better! 😱🍎 | Dr. Jason Fung


Could a simple, nutritious food help support your health as you age better than relying on another supplement? As we get older, maintaining healthy muscles, restful sleep, strong bones, and steady energy becomes increasingly important. Magnesium plays a vital role in hundreds of processes throughout the body, but the best approach to nutrition after 60 involves more than just taking a pill. In this educational video, we explore magnesium glycinate, magnesium-rich foods, and how everyday dietary choices may support healthy aging.

Discover why whole foods deserve a place in your daily routine, how magnesium contributes to normal muscle and nerve function, and what older adults should know before changing their supplement habits. We also discuss the importance of evidence-based nutrition, individual needs, and consulting a healthcare professional before stopping prescribed treatments or supplements.

00:00 – 🚨 The magnesium mistake many seniors overlook

15:05 – 🥗 How to include magnesium-rich foods in your diet  
17:20 – ⚠️ Supplement safety and medication considerations  
19:15 – 🌿 Building sustainable healthy habits  
20:30 – ❤️ Final advice for vitality and longevity
